chapters.title: The Useful Discontent
pages: On the Monday Emma Vale decided she could no longer bear her job, she spent seven hours making a colour-coded plan to deliver it.

The plan concerned a new customer-accounts system for a national utilities company: three teams, two suppliers, one deadline that had already moved twice. Emma was good at this sort of work. She could identify the person who had not read the meeting papers, the risk no one wanted recorded, and the decision that would later be remembered as having been obvious. At thirty-two, she was a senior project manager, though her title suggested a grandeur her days rarely possessed. Most mornings she translated other people’s urgency into boxes on a screen.

At 4.18 she found a discrepancy between the supplier’s estimate and the internal budget. It was not catastrophic. It was exactly the kind of discrepancy that became catastrophic if everyone agreed to call it harmless. She sent a careful note to Rachel, her manager, and waited.
Rachel appeared beside Emma’s desk at six, coat over one arm. She was in her forties, brisk without being cruel, and had the rare quality of remembering what people had said when they were tired.
“You’re right,” she said, reading the figures. “I’ll take it to Finance tomorrow. Don’t stay late to make the spreadsheet prettier.”
“I wasn’t going to.”
Rachel looked at the colour-coded tabs. “Of course not.”

They smiled, but Emma felt the familiar irritation beneath her own laugh: she had become reliable enough to be teased about her reliability. Her salary was £52,000 a year. After tax, pension contributions and other deductions, roughly £3,200 reached her current account each month. She rented a one-bedroom flat in Bristol, paid £1,180 in rent, and had no debt beyond the ordinary, forgettable kind: a phone contract and a credit card she cleared every month. Her personal monthly costs, including rent, bills, food, travel and a modest social life, averaged £1,650. She knew this because she had once built a spreadsheet to find out whether she could afford to reduce her hours. She had never used it for that purpose.
In the evening she met Priya at a restaurant near the station. Priya, a freelance illustrator, arrived with rain on her fringe and a cardboard tube of drawings under one arm.
“You look as though you’ve just discovered a new category of risk,” Priya said.
“I’m tired of managing projects I don’t believe in.”
“That’s different from being tired.” Priya unfolded her napkin. “Do you believe in any of them?”

Emma considered this. There were people on the project she respected, and customers who needed the system to work. She did not despise the work. That was part of the difficulty. Her dissatisfaction had no villain, only a steady accumulation: meetings about meetings, careful recommendations diluted into acceptable ones, and the peculiar fatigue of making things happen without feeling that anything had become more real.

“I keep thinking about a shop,” she said. “A small one. Properly chosen things—stationery, home goods, gifts, all made by people around here. Not a row of identical candles with a local label stuck on. Workshops, too. Printing, mending, maybe bookbinding. Events that don’t require everyone to be brilliant at networking.”
Priya’s face softened, which Emma mistook for agreement. “That sounds like you.”
“You mean organised?”
“I mean you notice what people need when they say they’re fine.” Priya paused. “But a lovely idea and a viable shop are not the same thing.”
“I know.”
“Do you?”
Emma took a drink. “I’m not proposing to resign tomorrow.”
That, she realised as she said it, was not quite an answer.

At home she opened a fresh document and typed THE SHOP at the top. She listed what she thought she knew. Bristol had independent makers, but their products were scattered among fairs, studios and online accounts. People wanted gifts that felt personal without being sentimental. A shop could give customers a place to discover them, while paid workshops and community events could make it more than a retail room. She wrote down a possible monthly sales figure: £18,000. It looked reassuringly round. She wrote “average gross margin 48%” beneath it, having chosen a number that seemed plausible from a few online articles and two conversations with shop owners.
She did not yet know that a margin was not profit, or that an attractive assumption could be made to look like a fact simply by putting it in a table.
The next morning Rachel asked her to lead the next phase of the system project, which would last at least a year.
“It’s good work,” Rachel said. “More authority, more visibility. And, candidly, you’d be hard to replace.”
The compliment was generous. It also landed like a door being held open into a room Emma had already begun to leave.
“I’d like to think about it.”
“You should. Think about the job, not just the week you’ve had.”

Emma nodded. She respected Rachel too much to pretend the warning was unkind. That evening she added a new line to her document: Do not confuse escape with a plan. Then, beneath it, she wrote another: Find out what people will actually pay for.
For the first time in months, the work ahead felt difficult in a way that belonged to her.

chapters.title: What People Said
pages: Emma began with the people most likely to be polite.

She sent a short questionnaire to former colleagues, neighbours, friends of friends and the members of a local makers’ group. It asked what they bought as gifts, where they found local products, and whether they would attend workshops in a shop. She included an open question about what the city lacked. The answers arrived quickly, generous with adjectives: lovely, needed, brilliant, overdue.
“I’d absolutely come,” wrote one former colleague. Another said the concept was “exactly what Bristol needs”. A third asked whether Emma could hold a launch event in the spring.
The responses were pleasant enough to encourage a person into trouble. Only one asked for the price of anything.
Priya came over on Saturday to read the results. Emma had printed them and arranged them on the kitchen table as if the paper might reveal a more substantial answer if laid out in order.
“You’ve asked whether they like the idea,” Priya said. “You haven’t asked them to choose it over something else.”
“I asked what they buy.”
“You asked what they remember buying. There’s a difference.”
Emma bristled. She knew the distinction; she had spent years testing assumptions for a living. But the people answering were her friends, and she did not want to treat their kindness as bad data.
Priya tapped one response. “This person says they’d attend a printmaking workshop. Did they book one?”
“It was a survey.”
“Exactly.”

Emma looked again at the answers. People praised independent shops and then ordered birthday presents from large websites because they were reliable, open late and easy to return. They said they wanted local products, but could not name a price they would pay for a notebook or a bowl. Emma had spent a week admiring the warmth of the replies and only now noticed their cost: none.

She tried a second method. Over the next fortnight she spoke to twenty-four people outside independent shops and markets, making clear that she was researching rather than selling. She asked what they had bought, how much they had paid, and what had made them walk in.

People were more specific in person, though not always more useful. A woman who bought most of her gifts online said she liked browsing in shops but hated feeling watched. A man carrying a paper bag from a homeware chain said he would pay more for a locally made mug, then admitted he had never done so. A mother wanted workshops that her teenager would not consider “for children”. Two people said they would attend events if they were free.
Emma wrote down the last answer and asked what sort of event they meant.
“Just something nice,” one woman said. “A talk or a little demonstration. Nothing too organised.”
Emma did not write down that such an event would still require a person to organise it.

She also visited other businesses. At a design shop near the city centre, the owner, Yasmin, allowed Emma to ask questions after the afternoon rush. Yasmin had been trading for nine years. Her shop was orderly but not austere; the shelves held jewellery, ceramics and paper goods, each item labelled with its maker.

“People tell me they want local,” Yasmin said, “but they want a receipt, a refund and the confidence that the thing will arrive before Saturday. You have to make the local part convenient, not make convenience sound like a moral failure.”
“How do you decide what to stock?”

“I ask what sells, then I ask whether I still want to be selling it in six months.” Yasmin turned a small ceramic dish in her hands. “I’ve got suppliers I love whose work barely moves. If I buy too deeply because I admire them, I can’t pay them promptly. That isn’t ethical. It’s vanity with a nice story attached.”
Emma wrote this down, though she disliked how plainly it applied to her.

The following week, she tested a possible workshop with a local printmaker named Leon. He offered a two-hour introductory session, materials included. They agreed that the test would be advertised through a neighbourhood mailing list, with a booking fee of £28 and a minimum of six participants. Emma would handle bookings and refreshments; Leon would teach and receive a set fee.
The mailing list owner posted the event. Sixteen people clicked through. Four bought tickets. One asked whether there was a discount for bringing a friend, then bought none.
Emma wanted to lower the price. Leon did not.
“If I charge less, I still use the same paper and spend the same afternoon,” he said. “I’m not saying people should pay whatever I ask. I’m saying the price needs to work for both of us.”

They ran the session with four participants. It was enjoyable, intimate and financially thin. After paying Leon’s agreed fee, buying tea and covering the room hire, Emma had lost £31. The loss was small enough to call research, but it had still come from her personal account.
On the walk home she felt embarrassed by her initial optimism and, more surprisingly, relieved. The number had finally told her something.
When she told Priya, Priya did not say she had been right.
“Would you do another?”
“Yes. But I’d need to test the price and the format properly.”
“And the shop?”
“I still want it.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”
Emma folded the event accounts into her notebook. “I don’t know yet.”

This time the answer felt less like retreat than accuracy. She could not build a business on the sentence people used when they wanted to encourage her. She needed evidence that survived a payment screen.

chapters.title: The Price of Room
pages: Emma’s first version of the financial forecast was elegant and wrong.

She had assumed monthly sales of £18,000 and a gross margin of 48 per cent. That produced £8,640 in gross profit, a figure that seemed to leave room for rent, wages and all the rest. It did not. Her table treated workshop income as if it were retail sales, ignored card fees, delivery and packaging, and placed tax in a cell labelled “later”. She had counted her savings as if every pound were available for the business.
The problem became visible when she took the plan to Martin Shaw.

Martin had owned and managed two small retail businesses before becoming a volunteer mentor at a local enterprise centre. He had a reputation for asking a question, waiting, and then asking it again in a way that made the first answer sound like a rehearsed defence. Emma had met him through a business-planning session. He had agreed to review her assumptions over coffee.
He read the forecast without comment, then drew a line beneath the £18,000 figure.
“Where does this come from?”
“A rough estimate based on footfall, likely conversion and average transaction value.”
“Have you measured the footfall?”
“Not in the proposed street.”
“Have you measured conversion?”
“Not for my shop.”
“Then this isn’t an estimate. It’s a hope with arithmetic around it.”
Emma kept her expression level. “I know it needs testing.”
“Good. Now test it. And don’t call the money left after product cost profit. You still have rent, utilities, insurance, wages, card charges, repairs, tax, and the amount you need to live on.”

He turned the page. The retail gross margin, he explained, was sales revenue less the cost of goods sold, before operating expenses. It was not the cash left in her bank. Workshops required their own calculations: ticket revenue less tutor fees, materials, room use and payment charges. If she sold a £40 object for which she had paid the maker £20, that created £20 of gross profit, not £20 of net profit. If the object took six months to sell, the cash tied up in it mattered too.
“Your proposed rent is £2,100 a month,” Martin said. “What does the landlord require?”
“Three months’ rent as a deposit, plus the first month in advance. There may be legal fees.”
“So at least £8,400 before you unlock the door.”
Emma had calculated the deposit but had mentally kept it apart from the business, as if money paid to a landlord remained available because it might one day return.

Martin asked about fit-out. Emma had a broad allowance of £9,000 for shelving, lighting, paint, counters, signage and basic work. He made her divide it into essential, deferrable and attractive. A compliant electrical check and secure storage belonged in the first category. Custom joinery and a handmade counter did not. Initial stock was another £8,000 in her draft, a mixture she had invented without supplier quotes.
“And your savings?” he asked.
“All of it?”
“No.”
“Good. What remains for you?”

Emma paused. Her personal costs averaged £1,650 a month. She could not responsibly spend all her savings on a shop and assume she would draw a wage immediately. She had thought of her salary as a bridge she would leave behind; Martin made her see that it had also been the source of a safety margin.

They rebuilt the outline. The planned shop’s monthly fixed costs would include £2,100 rent, estimated utilities and business rates, insurance, broadband, bookkeeping and basic software. Some costs, such as card fees, packaging, materials and stock, would vary with sales. A part-time employee would be a later decision, not a line to soothe her into believing she could be everywhere at once.

Emma added an owner’s draw to the forecast. Martin insisted she distinguish it from business expenses in her working model: it was still cash she would need personally, even if the accounting treatment differed. She added a separate tax reserve for any taxable profit or other liabilities her accountant later confirmed. Money set aside for tax could not be used as working capital merely because it remained in the current account.
“A forecast is not a promise,” Martin said. “It’s a way of noticing what would have to be true.”
She left with less confidence in her original idea and more confidence in the questions she needed to answer.
That evening Emma called her parents. Her mother was pleased, then frightened; her father asked what would happen if the shop failed.
“I’d look for another job,” Emma said.
“After what?” he asked.
“After learning something.”
He was quiet for a moment. “That sounds better than saying it can’t fail.”

Her parents lived outside Bath and had not saved money for her to spend. They had helped with her university costs and were still paying off the last of their mortgage. Emma was grateful that they did not offer a loan. She did not want affection to become a liability they could not afford.

Later she looked at her savings statement. £42,000 remained a substantial sum until it had to serve several purposes at once: business set-up, stock, living costs, emergencies and the future. She began a new worksheet with separate balances for personal reserve, set-up costs, opening stock and working capital. The categories did not create money. They did prevent her from pretending one pound could do four jobs.

chapters.title: A Room for Testing
pages: The evidence did not tell Emma to abandon the shop. It told her to stop asking the evidence to approve it.

She proposed a three-week pop-up in a vacant unit managed by a local arts organisation. The rent was £650 for the period, including basic utilities; the organisation also required public liability insurance and a small refundable key deposit. The unit was on a side street rather than the high-footfall route Emma had imagined. Its low rent made it a useful test, but its location meant she could not pretend the results would predict every other shop.

She wrote a short plan: twelve local makers, a narrow product range, a weekend workshop, and a simple record of visitors, transactions, average transaction value, questions and stock movement. She would not buy products outright from every maker. For a few items, she negotiated sale-or-return terms; for others, she bought modest quantities at wholesale prices. She agreed payment dates clearly and recorded consignment stock separately from stock she owned.

Not every maker accepted the terms. One potter wanted a larger opening order than Emma could afford. Another was uneasy about sale-or-return because it transferred too much risk to her. Emma disliked saying no, then disliked herself for disliking it. She could not call a relationship fair simply because it made her feel generous.
She told the potter, Mo, that she could take six pieces at wholesale or display a small number on consignment, with weekly sales reporting and payment on a set date.
“I can’t produce a separate box of work for each shop,” Mo said. “If you don’t buy enough, it may not be worth the packing.”
“I understand.”
“Do you?” His voice was tired, not hostile. “Everyone likes supporting makers until we ask them to carry the cost.”

Emma had no persuasive reply. They agreed she would collect the six pieces herself, avoiding a delivery charge. It was a small adjustment, but one grounded in Mo’s actual constraints rather than the moral language of her plan.

The pop-up opened on a wet Thursday. Emma had spent the previous evening correcting labels she had already printed and rearranging the front table three times. She had chosen a restrained palette, paper goods and household objects, and displayed prices plainly. Priya had helped paint a sign but refused to let Emma describe the shop as “a platform for the creative community”.
“It sounds as though you’re trying to rent them,” Priya said.
“What should I call it?”
“A shop that sells their work. You can be proud of that without pretending you’re doing everyone a favour.”

For the opening, Emma had expected acquaintances and received more acquaintances than customers. Several praised the windows. One asked whether the workshop was free. A woman bought a £9 card and asked for a receipt. Emma’s professional instincts told her to study every interaction, while her personal instincts told her to treat each visitor as a vote on her worth.

By the second day, she had learned to ask whether someone was looking for a gift or something for themselves. She did not hover. She also stopped saying “just browsing” on their behalf, a habit she had acquired from shops where staff seemed to fear an empty silence.

An awkward moment came when a customer returned a small tray after discovering a crack beneath its felt feet. Emma’s first impulse was to explain that the maker had supplied it in that condition only a few hours earlier. She swallowed the defence, apologised, and offered a refund or replacement.
“I like it,” the customer said. “I don’t want to be difficult.”
“You’re not. It should have been checked before it reached you.”

Emma refunded the £32, then messaged the maker privately with a photograph and a clear description. She did not accuse him in front of the customer, and she did not treat the refund as a cost she could ignore. The item had been sold on consignment, so the settlement needed adjusting. The conversation was uncomfortable and practical. It ended with the maker agreeing to inspect the remaining trays and Emma adding a basic quality check to her receiving notes.
That evening she entered the refund, the sale, and the stock adjustment. The figures did not resemble the clean promise of her first forecast. They were more useful.

The pop-up produced modest results. Visitors came in, but many did not buy. Customers who did spend tended to buy one or two items rather than fill a basket. The workshop sold seven tickets at £28 after Emma changed the wording and showed the materials and finished example clearly. It covered Leon’s fee, materials and card charges, with a small contribution towards the pop-up’s overhead. It was not a dependable profit centre yet.

The shop sold £3,960 of retail goods over three weeks, including the weekend workshop income separately recorded. The retail gross margin was close to the planned 48 per cent, though the mix varied; some products carried a higher margin, while others were priced to leave makers a fair share. Gross profit did not pay the pop-up rent, insurance, transport, Emma’s time or her living costs.
On the final afternoon, Priya arrived with coffee and read the sales sheet.
“What have you learned?”
“That people will buy some of it. That the workshop needs clearer value. That the shop can’t be built on compliments.”
“And what have you not learned?”
Emma looked at the narrow street outside. “Whether this works at £2,100 rent.”
Priya nodded. It was not a discouraging answer. It was the one Emma had earned.

chapters.title: Notice
pages: At the end of the pop-up, Emma returned the key and carried the unsold stock home in labelled boxes. A few makers collected their pieces; others agreed to leave them with her for the next test. She paid every supplier according to their terms before making any new purchases. It made the remaining cash look smaller, but more honest.

The figures showed that retail sales had been uneven. Saturday was busy and converted well; two weekday afternoons were nearly empty. The £3,960 in retail revenue had produced roughly £1,900 in gross profit before the pop-up’s fixed costs and other expenses. The workshop had covered its direct costs and contributed modestly. None of that was a forecast for a full shop. It was a set of observations from one location, one season and a short period.

Emma had started with £42,000 in savings. The pop-up, research, samples and travel had reduced the total, though much of the product stock she had purchased remained saleable. She kept the personal and business accounts separate. Her personal reserve was not available to patch a weak trading month without a deliberate decision. Working capital had its own purpose: paying suppliers, rent, bills and ordinary operating costs while sales arrived unpredictably. A tax reserve was a further set-aside, not a reward for being profitable.
Martin reviewed the results at the enterprise centre. He did not congratulate her for having completed the test.
“Your starting sales assumption was £18,000 a month,” he said. “What would have to happen to reach it?”
“More customers, a higher conversion rate, repeat business, workshop income.”
“Those are categories, not mechanisms.”

Emma opened her notebook. She had counted visitors at the pop-up, but some had returned more than once. She had not separated first visits from repeat visits, and her estimate of conversion depended on staff remembering to tick marks during busy spells. The average transaction value was lower than she had expected. Her range included many thoughtful objects priced under £30, but customers were not buying enough of them to create the weekly revenue she would need.
“I could add more expensive pieces,” she said.
“Could you sell them? Would your customers want them? Would you be willing to hold the stock?” Martin asked. “Don’t solve a cash problem by decorating it with a bigger item.”

They worked through the proposed premises. Rent would be £2,100 each month, before utilities and the other fixed costs. The landlord required three months’ rent as a deposit and one month in advance: £8,400 before legal fees. Emma’s reduced fit-out estimate, after separating essential work from the attractive extras, was £7,200. A cautious opening-stock budget of £6,500 was still significant, even with a mix of wholesale purchases and agreed consignment. Insurance, signs, accounting support, small equipment and pre-opening costs would add more.

Her savings were not sufficient for every desirable version of the plan and a comfortable personal runway. They might support a lean opening if she protected a personal reserve, kept fit-out disciplined and did not over-order. But the monthly sales needed to cover business costs, her draw and tax obligations were not yet demonstrated.
“You could wait,” Martin said. “You could also take a smaller unit, negotiate a shorter lease, or test more events. A lease is not courage. It is a commitment with terms.”
Emma knew he was right. She also knew she was tired of treating postponement as if it were automatically the sensible choice.
She discussed it with Rachel on a walk beside the river. The system project had entered a stable phase, and Rachel had offered Emma the lead role she had mentioned before.
“I don’t want to tell you to stay because I need you,” Rachel said. “That would be a poor reason for you to give me.”
“The job is good.”

“It is. You’re good at it. Those facts don’t require you to stay forever.” Rachel watched a cyclist pass. “But if you leave, don’t pretend that a shop is automatically more honest than a company. You’ll still have targets. You’ll still make decisions that disappoint people. They’ll just be yours.”
Emma had expected to be defended or persuaded. Instead, Rachel had given her the less comforting gift of treating her as an adult.
“I’ve been offered the lead role,” Emma said. “I think I have to decline it.”
“Then give me enough notice to plan properly.”
“I will.”
They returned to the office without resolving whether the choice was wise. Emma wrote her resignation letter that evening and did not send it.
Priya listened the next day while Emma described the rent, deposit, fit-out, stock and the money she intended to keep untouched for personal costs.
“I’m concerned,” Priya said. “Not because I think you’ll fail. Because you keep describing the worst case as though you’ll simply get another job and feel fine.”
“I can’t know what it would feel like.”
“No. But you can decide what you’re willing to lose.”

Emma looked at the boxes of remaining stock stacked by the wall. She had wanted Priya to say that she would help with the shop, as though friendship could be transformed into free labour without negotiation. Instead, Priya offered to design a small printed map of the makers for a proper fee, once Emma had a budget. Emma was embarrassed by the thought she had not quite admitted to herself, and grateful that Priya had not allowed it to become an expectation.

Two weeks later, after reviewing the figures again and speaking to an accountant about the structure and tax obligations, Emma declined Rachel’s offer and gave formal notice. Her final working day would be six weeks away. She did not sign a lease that afternoon. She arranged a second pop-up in a different neighbourhood, this time with a clearer workshop offer and a modest budget. She asked the landlord of the proposed unit whether a shorter initial term or a break clause was possible, and requested the full costs in writing.
The decision did not feel like a leap. It felt like signing a page that made the next page unavoidable.
At her desk, she cleared the drafts from the project folder and handed over the risk log to a colleague. Rachel came by before leaving.
“You’ve left good notes,” she said.
“I’ve had practice.”
“You have.”

Emma watched her go, then turned back to the list she had made for the shop. It contained no promise that the business would flourish, no guarantee that customers would prefer local goods once they saw the prices, and no way to know how much of her confidence was appetite and how much was fatigue. There was only a testable next step, an amount she could afford to spend, and a date by which she would examine the evidence again.
For now, that was enough to begin.

chapters.title: The Terms of the Room
pages: The notice had been sent; it did not, Emma discovered, make a shop appear. It made a succession of decisions impossible to postpone. On Monday morning she sat opposite a commercial agent in a room with a glass table and no visible clock, while the proposed lease lay between them like a test she had not revised for.

The premises on Calder Street were promising in the manner of an old dog: appealing, imperfect and likely to require more care than its owner admitted. The front room had generous windows and a tiled floor worn smooth in the middle. Behind it, two smaller rooms might accommodate workshops and stock, though one contained a sink whose tap had been secured with a strip of tape. The agent described the building as having “character”. Emma wrote down “damp at rear wall” instead.

She had brought Martin, the solicitor recommended by a former colleague, and had expected his questions to sound fussy. Instead, each one revealed a different way in which her optimism might become someone else’s income. Who was responsible for the roof? Were the electrical circuits certified? Could the landlord require her to restore every alteration at the end of the term? Was the proposed rent review upward-only? What, precisely, did “reasonable repair” mean when the tenant inherited a property already in need of repair?
The agent, Mr Pritchard, folded his hands. “The landlord has no appetite for a lengthy negotiation.”

“Then perhaps he has an appetite for an empty property,” Emma said. Her voice was steadier than her pulse. “I’m not asking him to refurbish it. I’m asking not to be liable for defects that exist before I get the keys.”

Martin looked at her, faintly approving, and returned to the schedule of condition. They agreed that the landlord would address a leak around the rear window before occupation, while Emma would take responsibility for internal decoration and routine maintenance. The schedule would include photographs, dated and signed. She had thought of the lease as permission to begin. It was also a list of expensive things she must not accidentally promise.

The headline rent was £18,000 a year, payable quarterly in advance. The landlord wanted a deposit equal to three months’ rent, £4,500, and a five-year term. Emma had insisted on a break clause after three years, exercisable with six months’ notice, and on confirmation that the landlord would not unreasonably withhold consent for the shop’s proposed use. The agent objected to the break clause as “unusual”. Martin pointed out that unusual was not the same as impossible.

Rates were less easily settled. The property’s current rating information suggested a small-business rates bill, but the final liability depended on the assessment and on Emma’s eligibility for relief. She entered the full estimate in her cash-flow forecast rather than assuming relief would arrive. Utilities, meanwhile, would be metered separately; the old boiler might make the winter gas bill less charming than the agent’s description of the room.

Insurance would include public liability, employers’ liability once she hired anyone, contents cover and cover for business interruption, though the last item required careful scrutiny of what counted as an interruption. Martin’s fee, the agent’s administration charge and the surveyor’s inspection together added several thousand pounds to the sum she had imagined spending on “the legal bits”. She revised the forecast at the table, not later, and watched her available working capital contract.

The forecast still showed enough cash to proceed, but not enough to proceed carelessly. Emma separated the money into obligations: rent and deposit; professional fees; fit-out; opening stock; operating costs; and a tax reserve for VAT and income tax when they became relevant. Revenue, she reminded herself, would not be profit, and money in the till would not all be hers. The distinction had seemed obvious in a spreadsheet. It felt more serious beside a signature line.

On Wednesday she returned with a builder and a damp specialist. The rear wall was not a disaster, but the plaster needed to dry before it could be finished, and the electrical consumer unit was older than Emma. The builder could not promise a completion date until the electrician had inspected the circuits. His estimate was a range, not a fixed price. She resented the uncertainty, then recognised that resenting it would not turn it into certainty.

At the next meeting, Mr Pritchard offered a modest rent-free fit-out period, conditional on completion of the lease. Emma accepted only after Martin had written the dates into the agreement. She paid the deposit from the business account, not her personal account, and watched the transfer leave with a sensation like stepping off a kerb before checking for traffic.

Outside, the street was damp and ordinary. A delivery van blocked half the view of the windows. Emma stood inside the empty shop and measured the distance between the front door and the rear wall. She could picture shelves, a long worktable and people staying after a class to talk. She could also picture the meter running while the plaster dried.

For the first time, she understood that courage, in this particular venture, might mean refusing to confuse a promising room with a sound deal. The lease was signed. The room was hers to make useful, not to romanticise.

chapters.title: The Work Behind the Window
pages: The keys arrived on a wet Thursday, two days after Emma had imagined them arriving. The electrician found a fault in the rear circuit, the damp specialist asked for another week of drying, and the builder explained that his earlier estimate had not included replacing the cracked floor tiles beneath the old counter. None of this was dishonest. That was, in its way, more difficult: there was nobody to blame and no single conversation that could make the delays vanish.

Emma kept a notebook of decisions and costs. She wrote the date beside every estimate, marked which figures included VAT and which did not, and added a column for contingency. The contingency was not a separate pot of money so much as a warning that the other numbers were capable of changing.

Aisha Patel came to see the premises after Emma had advertised for a part-time shop and workshop organiser. They had met at an evening market where Aisha had been coordinating a ceramics demonstration, quietly redirecting a queue when the potter’s wheel stopped. Her application described experience in community arts administration, stock control and accessible event planning. It also included a sentence Emma had underlined: “A welcoming space needs clear systems, not merely warm intentions.”

Aisha wore a navy coat and carried a folder divided by coloured tabs. She inspected the rear room, asked about the sink, then wanted to know how many people the insurer would permit in a workshop. Emma, who had planned to ask her how she felt about the place, found herself answering questions she should already have settled.
“I’m not looking for a grand title,” Aisha said. “I need to know the hours, what I’m paid, and whether I’m being hired to run the workshops or to rescue every task that falls through the cracks.”

Emma explained the budget. She could offer twenty-four hours a week at £13.20 an hour, with paid holiday and statutory pension arrangements if applicable. The rate was above the legal minimum, but not generous. The initial contract would be for six months, with a review after three. Aisha listened without the gratitude Emma had, embarrassingly, expected.

“I can make that work,” she said. “But I’d want rotas four weeks ahead, and I’m not available every evening. My mother has appointments, and I do not want the job to assume that my life becomes flexible whenever the shop is busy.”
Emma agreed. Then she asked whether Aisha might cover late workshops “when necessary”. Aisha waited.
“Necessary can become a habit,” she said.

The pause was brief, but it altered the interview. Emma heard the old managerial reflex in her own question: convert a person’s goodwill into capacity before it has been offered. She wrote “evening cover agreed in advance” into her notes and asked Aisha what she thought the shop should open with.

“A smaller range than you’ve drawn,” Aisha said. She had looked at Emma’s draft plan: locally made ceramics, textiles, paper goods, pantry items and small homewares, arranged around a calendar of workshops. “If we have too many suppliers, we’ll spend all our time receiving and checking. And if every workshop is a different format, we won’t learn what customers actually want.”

Emma explained that breadth would make the selection feel curated rather than sparse. Aisha pointed out that breadth also meant cash tied up in stock. They did not reach agreement, but Emma found herself revising the list that evening. It was less satisfying than being told she had devised an excellent range and more useful.

Ben Collins, who made wooden kitchenware in a workshop outside the city, called before the end of the week. The previous batch of boards had sold well at the market research event, but his supplier of kiln-dried ash had raised prices, and a restaurant order had paid late. He needed a deposit to reserve materials for Emma’s opening order. He did not dress the request up as a favour.
“I can make fewer pieces,” he said. “Or we can agree a deposit and a later delivery date. I can’t hold the price on the whole range if my material cost has gone up.”

Emma’s first instinct was to ask for the original price. She had calculated her retail prices using the earlier quote and was already worried about the margin. Instead, she asked for a revised quotation showing materials, labour, delivery and payment dates. Ben sent it that afternoon. His wholesale price rose by eight per cent; the suggested retail price rose by less. The resulting gross margin would be thinner than Emma wanted, but the goods were well made and their provenance was verifiable.

They agreed a smaller first order, with a deposit of £420 and the balance due within fourteen days of delivery. Emma disliked reducing the range. She disliked more the thought of paying for more stock than she could afford to sell.

Meanwhile, Ruth Bell of Bell & Rowe, the established home-and-gift shop a few streets away, sent a note through the local traders’ association. She offered Emma the name of a reliable locksmith and warned her that the council would want clear access to the rear fire exit before workshops began. At their meeting, Ruth was friendly without being intimate.

“People say there’s room for every independent shop,” Ruth said, making a mark on her tea with the spoon. “Sometimes there is. Sometimes they mean they hope you’ll do well without taking any of their customers.”
Emma asked whether Ruth was worried about the new shop. Ruth considered the question. “I’m attentive,” she said. “That’s not the same as worried.”

The remark stayed with Emma. Competition, she had imagined, would be a clean line between two businesses. Ruth’s shop had regular customers, long-standing suppliers and its own account with the same local makers. The street was not a blank space waiting for Emma to improve it.

At the end of the week, Aisha accepted the job, subject to the written contract. The builder promised no opening date. Emma adjusted the launch plan again, moving the proposed workshops to the week after the shop opened. The windows were still bare. Behind them, people could see dust, ladders and a handwritten sign asking them to bear with the work.
It was not the polished beginning she had planned. It was, however, a beginning that had begun to account for other people.

chapters.title: The Cost of Almost Ready
pages: The first week of renovation produced more invoices than visible change. The electrician replaced the faulty circuit and upgraded the emergency lighting. The plumber repaired the sink, then found that the pipe behind it had been patched twice. The landlord’s contractor sealed the rear window, as promised, but the wall still needed time before it could be painted. Emma paid each supplier according to the agreed terms and kept copies in a folder Aisha labelled “Not Glamorous, Still Essential”.

Aisha had a gift for seeing the future in small failures. She noticed that the door closer swung too hard for someone carrying a bag, that the proposed workshop table would obstruct the route to the rear exit, and that Emma’s draft booking form asked about dietary requirements without explaining how the information would be used. Emma had been irritated by the questions until she realised that most of them had not occurred to her.

They met the council’s environmental health officer to discuss the planned events. The shop was not going to serve cooked food, but the pantry goods would need correct labelling and traceability, and any refreshments at workshops had to be handled safely. The officer was practical, not forbidding. She asked about hand-washing facilities, cleaning records, waste storage and the distinction between packaged products and food prepared on site.
“It’s better to ask now than after someone has made a complaint,” she said.

Emma wrote this down, although it sounded less like advice than an avoidable cost. She checked the council’s requirements for planning and permitted use as well. The lease allowed retail and small community workshops, but the details mattered: occupancy limits, fire arrangements, and whether the proposed class schedule crossed into a use requiring a different consent. Martin confirmed the interpretation in writing.

The workshop insurance required a risk assessment and a clear record of instructors’ qualifications. Aisha built the process into the booking system. Emma had intended to add forms once the first classes filled. Aisha explained that a system introduced after it became inconvenient was often a system nobody followed.
“You make everything sound as if it could become a liability,” Emma said.
“Some things can,” Aisha replied. “The point is not to be frightened of them. The point is to know which things we’ve agreed to carry.”

The equipment order arrived in stages. Shelving cost more than Emma’s initial estimate because the cheaper units were unstable when loaded. The card terminal required a monthly fee, and the payment provider charged a transaction fee that varied with the card type. The website’s booking function needed a small professional adjustment. Emma had hoped to manage it herself, but the developer’s fee was less than the cost of spending three days learning a system she would then have to maintain.

Stock was less straightforward than ordering equipment. Ben’s boards arrived on the date he had promised, beautifully finished and wrapped in recycled paper that resisted the shop’s labels. Aisha checked the delivery against the order, counted every piece, and found one board with a split at the handle. Ben apologised and offered either a replacement or a credit.

Emma initially asked him to replace it before opening. Aisha pointed out that the maker had already made two journeys to the shop, and the item could be sold at a reduced price if the defect was fully disclosed. Emma called Ben back. They agreed a £24 credit, with the board marked down and the flaw described on its tag. The customer would decide whether it was acceptable; the maker would not be asked to absorb an undisclosed defect.

The figures began to press on one another. Rent and service charges were fixed costs. Wages, insurance and the card terminal’s monthly fee would continue whether or not anyone came through the door. Packaging and card charges rose with sales; workshop materials varied according to enrolment. The cost of stock was not an immediate expense in the same way as rent, but it was cash tied up until the goods sold. Emma started tracking stock at cost and retail value separately, with a cautious allowance for items that might need discounting.

She also opened a separate tax reserve account. VAT registration would depend on taxable turnover, not on whether the business felt established, and her bookkeeper advised her to review the threshold monthly. Income tax and National Insurance were not the shop’s operating profit either, but cash she would eventually owe. Emma transferred a proportion of each week’s takings into the reserve, resisting the temptation to count it as available.

The first month’s cash-flow forecast now showed an opening balance lower than she had anticipated. There was enough to pay the remaining fit-out invoices, the balance on the first stock orders and the first quarter’s rent. There was not enough to absorb a long closure without changes. The difference between being solvent on paper and having cash on the day a bill arrived became a daily consideration.

At home, Emma’s sister Helen asked whether she was sleeping. Emma replied that she was, which was not quite true. Helen had once described Emma as someone who could turn a concern into a spreadsheet and then mistake the spreadsheet for resolution. Emma objected to the comparison. She noticed, later, that she had spent an hour colour-coding a forecast when what she needed was to ask the builder whether the plaster would be dry by Friday.

On Friday, it was not. They moved the soft-opening date by a week. Emma felt the embarrassment of changing a date she had already given people, then sent a clear update without blaming anyone. Aisha took responsibility for contacting the workshop participants. Two asked to keep their places; one requested a refund. Emma approved it promptly.

A week did not make the walls perfect. It did allow the paint to dry, the emergency lighting to be tested and the rear route to be cleared. The shelves stood upright. The booking system worked. The stock was modest and deliberately uneven, a selection rather than an inventory of every possible desire.

When Emma turned the key in the front door that evening, the shop smelt of fresh paint, cardboard and the coffee she had forgotten to finish. It was almost ready. The word almost had cost more than she had expected, and it still had work left to do.

chapters.title: The Door Opens
pages: They opened on a Saturday because the street was busiest then, not because Saturday promised success. Aisha had suggested a quiet preview for neighbours on Friday evening, but Emma had resisted the expense of another event until the first set of figures was clearer. In the end, they arranged a short invitation-only hour with tea from a local blender and no speeches. The choice felt practical, which did not prevent Emma from being nervous.

At eight on opening morning, she arrived to find Aisha already there, checking the till and moving a basket away from the accessible route. The front windows had been cleaned. A small board listed the day’s hours and the first three workshops, with prices and booking details. Emma had written “A new kind of local shop” on the draft sign. Aisha had crossed out “new kind of”. The final version simply said what the shop sold and when it was open.

The name, Common Thread, sat above the door in dark green lettering. Emma had worried that it sounded too earnest. Aisha said it sounded clear. They had agreed on a mix of locally made homewares, paper goods, textiles and a small pantry shelf, with the workshop table visible from the front. Not everything was local, but every product had a reason to be there, and the tags named makers rather than hiding them behind the shop’s branding.

At ten, the first customers came in: two friends who had seen the opening notice online and wanted to browse. One bought a pair of printed tea towels. The other asked whether the clay earrings were nickel-free, and Emma, unable to confirm it from the maker’s information, said she would check rather than guess. The customer thanked her and left without buying.

Emma found herself wanting to interpret the visit as a lost sale. Aisha wrote down the question and emailed the maker before noon. The answer came later that afternoon, with confirmation of the metal components. Aisha added the information to the product record and the display card. The customer returned the following week and bought the earrings.

By midday, the shop was full enough to feel lively and quiet enough to hear every exchange. People asked how the workshops worked, whether the makers were paid in advance, whether items could be wrapped, and whether Emma would stock a particular local ceramicist. Some stayed for twenty minutes and left empty-handed. A man examined three bowls, asked what made one more expensive than the others, and put all three back with care.

Emma’s original response to browsing had been to fill silence. She would point out the materials, the maker’s story, the local origin, the special finish. Aisha noticed that a customer who had turned towards the shelf was being given a biography. Later, when they were alone, she said, “They need room to decide whether they want to talk.”

Emma objected that people might not understand the selection without explanation. Aisha replied that the labels could explain what Emma did not need to say aloud. They looked at the labels together. Some were indeed small, crowded and self-congratulatory. Emma rewrote them that evening to include materials, care and maker, cutting the adjectives.

Ruth Bell came in just before closing. She moved slowly around the shop, looking at the display and the workshop table. Emma had prepared herself for a test, though Ruth did not behave as if she were conducting one.
“The windows are good,” Ruth said. “You can see the work happening.”
“That was the idea.”

“It’s a useful one. People like to know there’s somebody on the other side of the table.” Ruth bought a small notebook made by a printmaker she already stocked in a different format. “I hope you make it,” she added, and neither Emma nor Ruth pretended the sentence had only one meaning.

The till closed at six. Gross sales for the day were £1,146, including £190 from workshop bookings taken at the desk. That figure was revenue, not profit. The sales included VAT where applicable, and the day’s takings did not account for the cost of goods, card fees, wages, rent or the money already spent on setting the room up. Still, the number was real, and Emma let herself be pleased by it.

Aisha recorded refunds, card transactions and cash separately. They counted the till twice because Emma had entered one cash sale under the wrong product code. The mistake changed no money, but it changed the stock record. Emma felt foolish. Aisha showed her how to correct the transaction without deleting the audit trail.

The following week brought the first ordinary Tuesday. A drizzle settled over Calder Street, and for two hours no one came in. Emma checked the website, changed a photograph, checked the door, then wiped a counter that was already clean. Aisha began unpacking an order and asked whether Emma could help reconcile the delivery note. Emma said she would in a minute, then began composing a social-media post.

When Aisha finally took the reconciliation herself, Emma felt a small, unreasonable irritation. She had hired her to organise the shop, but the task had seemed like a test of care: surely the owner should be the one to ensure every item was counted. Aisha said nothing about the division of labour. She did, however, leave the delivery note beside Emma’s notebook, with one line highlighted: two packets of cards missing.

They contacted the supplier, who sent the missing stock two days later. The incident did not justify a theory about the supplier or the system. It justified checking deliveries before signing them off.

The first workshop, a bookbinding class with eight places, sold five. The instructor was paid the agreed fee; materials were charged separately and the booking fees covered the direct costs, though not the time Aisha had spent preparing the room. The participants were pleased. One posted a photograph. Three asked when the next class would be.

Emma went home tired and proud, then worried that pride might make her careless. Opening day had attracted attention. It had not established a pattern. The shop had received interest, purchases, questions and silence. Those were all forms of evidence, but none yet answered whether the business could support itself.

chapters.title: A Week Made of Small Things
pages: By the third week, Emma had learned that a shop could be quiet without being restful. When there were no customers, there were deliveries to check, stock to price, shelves to dust, a workshop to set up, receipts to reconcile and a dozen small messages that each appeared to require an immediate answer. The shop’s silence merely allowed every unfinished task to make itself heard.

Aisha put a rota on the wall and divided responsibilities between them. She would manage workshop bookings, delivery checks and the weekly stock report. Emma would handle supplier payments, bookkeeping with the external bookkeeper, marketing and the monthly review of sales. Cleaning was shared, as were customer-facing shifts. Emma agreed to the list and then repeatedly interrupted Aisha’s work to “help” with tasks Aisha had already been assigned.

On Monday, Emma re-labelled the pantry shelf because she thought the price cards looked inconsistent. On Tuesday, she changed the newsletter subject line after Aisha had scheduled it. On Wednesday, she took over a workshop booking call to explain the cancellation policy, although Aisha had written that policy and could explain it perfectly well.
At closing, Aisha said, “I can’t organise anything if the plan changes whenever you walk past.”
Emma’s first answer was that it was her shop. The phrase came out before she could improve it. Aisha looked at her, not offended so much as disappointed in the reasoning.
“Yes,” she said. “And you hired me to do the work you cannot do alone.”

Emma wanted to defend herself with the facts: she had paid for the shelves, taken the lease, carried the risk. Those facts were true and irrelevant. She could see that Aisha’s job had become a set of duties Emma might reclaim whenever she felt anxious. She apologised, though the apology did not make her habits disappear. They agreed that changes to scheduled work would be discussed rather than made silently. Emma added a rule for herself: if a task was delegated, she would ask about its progress before redoing it.

The figures from the first four weeks were mixed. Revenue was £8,420, including workshop bookings and product sales. After VAT collected was separated from income, the cost of goods sold came to £4,780. The gross profit was therefore £3,640, a gross margin of a little over forty-three per cent. Card fees and packaging reduced the contribution further. Rent, wages, utilities, insurance, software and other fixed or semi-fixed costs had not yet been covered by the gross profit.

The shop had not made an operating profit. Emma wrote that sentence at the top of the monthly report, then resisted the urge to call the month a failure. Some opening costs were exceptional; some were not. The rent would recur. Wages would recur. Stock would need replenishing, and tax reserves could not be raided simply because the bank balance looked reassuring after a good Saturday.

The cash position was tighter than the revenue figure suggested. Cash had gone into the lease deposit, professional fees, renovation, equipment and initial stock. Some of the stock remained on the shelves, still an asset at cost but not money available to pay the next rent instalment. Emma had paid suppliers on time, transferred the agreed amount to the tax reserve, and kept a working-capital buffer in the business account. The buffer was smaller than she wanted but had not been breached.

The bookkeeper, Moira, reviewed the accounts with them by video call. She pointed out that the workshop revenue needed to be separated from product sales for useful analysis, and that Emma should not treat the full booking payment as hers before the instructor and materials were paid. She also queried a batch of receipts Emma had photographed but not attached to transactions.
“You cannot expect the accounts to remember what you meant,” Moira said.

Emma spent the next morning attaching the receipts. The work was dull and oddly clarifying. Each transaction had a date, purpose and place in the month. She found one duplicate card charge from a supplier and recovered it, not because she had been brilliant but because the reconciliation made it visible.

Customer service proved less tidy. A woman returned a linen apron after the first wash, saying the colour had faded. The care label had advised a cool wash, and the woman had followed it. Emma offered a replacement or refund without first asking the supplier what she thought. The item’s maker explained that the fabric had been dyed in a small batch and that some fading was expected, though it should not have been so pronounced.

Emma felt protective of the maker and, at the same time, responsible to the customer. She refunded the full price, including the card transaction, and told the maker she would pause sales of that batch until they agreed on accurate care information. The refund reduced the week’s revenue. It also prevented the customer from being made to pay for a claim neither of them could substantiate.

Ben visited with a small top-up order. He told Emma that his restaurant client had paid at last, but his supplier had raised the price of the ash again. He could no longer guarantee the old wholesale rate. Emma asked whether a different wood would be suitable. They discussed durability, origin and price, then agreed that he would offer a beech version at a lower cost and explain the difference on the label. No one pretended this solved the pressure on his workshop. It did give both businesses a decision they could live with.

At the end of the day, Emma wrote the following week’s schedule. Aisha had asked for two evenings free, and they were there in ink. The next workshop had six bookings out of ten places. The most popular product was a stack of locally printed greeting cards with a modest margin and a quick turnover. The handmade ceramics had drawn admiration but sold slowly. Emma was tempted to order more of what looked beautiful; the sales report suggested she should first ask customers which pieces they actually wanted.

She began to see the distinction between a curated shop and a shop arranged around its owner’s preferences. Curation could include conviction, but conviction did not absolve her from noticing what people bought, what they returned, what they asked for and what they could not afford.

Before closing, Aisha put a cloth in Emma’s hand and pointed to the dust beneath the workshop table. Emma laughed, then cleaned it. She did not feel transformed. She felt tired, chastened and slightly more competent than she had been that morning.

Outside, Calder Street was settling into evening. Inside, the figures were still uncertain, the walls still imperfect, and the next month’s bills still due. Emma locked the door, checked it twice, and went home without reopening the spreadsheet on her phone.

chapters.title: The Saturday That Lied
pages: The market organiser had promised a good footfall, which was not the same thing as a good day’s trading. Emma knew the distinction. She had once used it in a presentation about customer acquisition, before she had known what it felt like to stand behind a counter while rain softened the paper labels on her stock. Still, when the city’s autumn makers’ trail brought a queue to the shop door on Saturday morning, she stopped distinguishing.

The trail had been advertised across the city, with printed maps and a programme of demonstrations. Emma had agreed to host a short session with ceramicist Nisha Patel, who would show visitors how she shaped a small pinch pot. The shop had not been chosen as a destination so much as placed on a route between the old library and a bakery. Yet people came in, damp-haired and curious, carrying the map. They bought Nisha’s cups, Mara’s linen napkins, and the small-batch preserves Emma had previously worried were too expensive for casual shoppers.

By eleven, the counter had become a surface for bags, receipts and abandoned umbrellas. A woman in a rust-coloured coat asked whether the carved wooden spoons were made in the city. Emma said they were made in the next county, by a maker who sourced fallen ash locally. The woman looked relieved, as if Emma had passed an examination, and bought two. Another customer asked whether the workshop fee included materials. It did, Emma said, and sold a place for the next month.

When the card terminal briefly lost its connection, Emma entered transactions on the paper backup sheet and let customers take their purchases with a promise to process payment once the signal returned. She disliked the informality, but the queue had grown to the door and she could not make everyone wait while she reset the router. At the end of the afternoon she had processed £2,940 in sales, of which £2,760 had been card payments and £180 cash. Her usual Saturday revenue was closer to £900.

At closing, she and Priya, who worked three days a week, counted stock and swept clay dust from the floor. Priya had been hired for her calmness; she could explain the difference between a hand-thrown bowl and a moulded one without making the second sound inferior. She looked at the sales report and raised her eyebrows.
“It was a good day,” Emma said.
“It was,” Priya agreed. “It was also a day with six hundred people on the trail.”
Emma smiled as though the qualification were a joke. “We should be ready for the next one.”

The figures seemed to support her. On a weighted average basis, the shop’s gross margin was about forty-two per cent: revenue less the direct cost of the goods sold, before rent, wages, utilities, insurance and the rest. The day’s sales therefore represented roughly £1,235 in gross profit. That was not net profit, and she knew it. But after months of explaining slow sales to herself, she wanted the number to mean something less provisional.

The card settlement would arrive on Tuesday, after the processor’s fee. The £180 in notes and coins had gone straight into the till float, not into the bank. Most of the stock sold had been bought on thirty-day terms, and its invoices were already approaching. The event had produced revenue immediately, but it had not produced usable cash in the same moment. Emma understood each sentence separately. She failed to let them alter her conclusion.

On Monday she emailed her suppliers. She ordered deeper quantities of the products that had sold, including the carved spoons, Nisha’s cups and the preserves. She added two new lines: wool throws from a small mill and a set of hand-painted cards. The orders came to £4,860, more than twice the previous month’s replenishment. She told herself that bulk ordering would reduce delivery costs and that customers had shown her what they wanted.

The workshop calendar was next. Emma had previously scheduled two sessions a month, each capped at eight participants. She added a second date to the pottery workshop, then another session on visible mending. She would need an extra table, more materials and someone to help clear up. The fees, she calculated, would cover the costs if each session filled to at least six places. It seemed prudent to test demand while it was present.
Priya read the revised calendar at the till. “Have you asked Nisha about two sessions?”
“I’ve emailed her.”
“And the mending teacher?”
“I’m confirming today.”
Priya paused. “You said we’d review the first two workshops before adding more.”
Emma heard the reminder as resistance. “We have reviewed them. People asked for more dates.”
“Three people asked,” Priya said. Her voice was even, but her hands had stopped folding tissue paper.
“Three people who were in the shop.” Emma opened the booking page on her laptop. “We can’t treat interest as evidence of nothing.”
“No. We can’t treat it as evidence of everything either.”

Emma did not answer. She had a list of orders to send and the familiar sensation of being back in a meeting where someone’s caution might be mistaken for lack of ambition. That comparison was unfair. Priya was not obstructing a strategy; she was noticing its assumptions. Emma placed the orders anyway.

On Tuesday the card settlement arrived: £2,690 after fees and adjustments. The till cash had been banked the previous evening. The bank balance looked briefly healthier, then the supplier payment run took £2,100. Rent was due the following week, wages on Friday, and VAT was not yet due but the portion she ring-fenced each month was not hers to spend. She moved the tax reserve into its separate account as usual, then stared at the remaining working capital.

The new orders would not all arrive at once, she thought. Some suppliers were slow. She had time. She had learned to distinguish cash from profit; she had not yet learned that a busy day could make her careless about the interval between them.
That evening, she wrote the event’s sales figure in the notebook she kept by the bed. Beneath it she wrote: repeatable demand. In the morning, she crossed out neither word.

chapters.title: A Promise on the Booking Page
pages: The first complaint arrived before the new workshops had begun, which Emma regarded as bad timing rather than useful information.

Mrs Finch came into the shop shortly after opening, carrying a paper bag by its twisted handles. She had booked two places on the visible-mending workshop and bought a small ceramic serving dish at the autumn trail. She set the bag on the counter and took out the dish, wrapped in a tea towel.
“There’s a crack along the foot,” she said. “I noticed it when I washed it.”

Emma examined the dish. The crack was narrow, but it ran far enough beneath the glaze that the piece might not be safe to use. The maker’s label had said that each piece was individually fired and that small irregularities were part of the process. Emma had sometimes leaned on that wording too heavily. Character was not a defence against a structural fault.
“I’m sorry. That shouldn’t have been sold as sound.”

“It was sold as a serving dish. I didn’t buy a decorative object.” Mrs Finch’s expression was controlled, though her mouth had tightened. “And I’d like the workshop money back. I can’t make the new date you moved us to.”

Emma’s first impulse was to correct her. The workshop date had not been moved; a second date had been added. The original session remained in place. Mrs Finch had booked the later one, which Emma had postponed when the teacher said she could not attend. The replacement date was a fortnight later, but the booking page had not been updated before an automated reminder went out showing the old time.
“That’s our mistake,” Emma said. “The reminder shouldn’t have said the first date.”

“It isn’t the only mistake. When I booked, the page said the workshop was for beginners and all materials were provided. I asked by email whether you’d have larger needles. I didn’t get an answer. Then I phoned and left a message.”

Emma felt the familiar heat of shame turn, almost immediately, into defence. She remembered the week: the event, the orders, a delivery arriving without its packing list. She did not remember the message. “I’m sorry no one got back to you.”
“I’ve brought the dish because it’s clearly defective. I’d like you to refund that too.” Mrs Finch’s gaze stayed on Emma. “I don’t want a store credit.”

The request was reasonable. The manner was not gentle. Mrs Finch spoke as if Emma had deliberately taken money for a faulty object and then concealed a changed appointment. Emma noticed her own urge to punish that severity by becoming precise, to distinguish every promise from every misunderstanding. It would have protected her pride and worsened the customer’s experience.
“I can refund the dish and both workshop places,” she said. “I’ll also cover the postage if you’d rather not carry it back.”
“I’ve already carried it here.”

“Of course. I’m sorry.” Emma processed the refunds. The dish had cost £38; the two workshop places were £72. The card terminal showed the transactions as pending. She wrote Mrs Finch’s name and the refund references on a receipt, then asked whether the woman wanted to wait while she checked the booking record.
“I want to know whether the workshop is actually happening.”
“It is,” Emma said. “But I can understand why you wouldn’t want to rely on that.”
Mrs Finch took the receipt. “I’m not trying to make your life difficult.”
“I don’t think you are.”
“It may not sound like it.”

There was a small, uncomfortable pause. Emma could have said that it did sound like it. She could also see that Mrs Finch had paid for two things and received uncertainty in return. “I’m glad you told me,” she said, and meant it less warmly than she wanted to.

After the customer left, Emma checked the booking system. The page showed the extra sessions but did not explain which dates were confirmed. The automated reminders had been generated from the original schedule. In her inbox she found Mrs Finch’s message, marked unread beneath a supplier invoice. Her telephone notes were in a drawer, but there was no record of the call. The phrase she had used at the event—“We’ll be in touch”—had promised a response without assigning one.
Priya listened while Emma described it. “The dish needs to go back to Nisha.”
“Yes. I’ll photograph it and ask her to inspect it.”
“And the booking page?”
“I’ll fix it.”
Priya kept her eyes on the booking ledger. “Who’s going to answer the messages?”
The question landed harder than accusation would have. Emma had added sessions and stock without adding a process to support either. “We’ll make a rota,” she said.
“We already have a rota.”
Emma looked at her. “I mean for enquiries.”
“Then we need to decide who owns it, and when cover is needed. I can’t be responsible for messages on the days I’m not here unless it’s in my hours.”
“You’re right.” Emma said it too quickly, trying to end the feeling rather than absorb it. She opened the diary and found a blank page.

They agreed that every enquiry would be entered in one shared log with the date received, the person responsible, a reply deadline and the outcome. Emma would review it at opening and closing; Priya would answer during her shifts. Workshop places would not be moved without direct contact with each participant. The website would show dates only after the teacher confirmed them. A clear cancellation policy would explain when refunds were available, though it could not replace ordinary judgment when the shop had made the error.

Emma also wrote a short note to Nisha with photographs of the cracked foot. She did not call it a manufacturing defect before the maker had inspected it. She did not call it an acceptable irregularity either. In the message she explained what the customer had reported and asked how they should assess the piece together.

That evening, the booking page was corrected. Emma added a line promising replies within two working days, then hesitated. A promise was easy to type and difficult to staff. She reduced the wording to: “We aim to reply within two working days; if your question is urgent, please telephone the shop.” It was not elegant. It was more honest.

The refunds reduced the day’s cash by £110 once the pending card transactions settled. They did not erase the mistake. Emma wrote them into the sales record as refunds, not as an inconvenience outside the accounts. She had built her shop around objects whose makers’ names she could say. She was beginning to understand that accountability also had to be made visible, even when it was less attractive than a hand-thrown glaze.

chapters.title: Thirty Days, More or Less
pages: Ben’s delivery was due on Wednesday. On Thursday morning, Emma sent a polite message asking whether he had an estimated arrival time. On Friday, he called.
“I’m not going to make the delivery this week,” he said. “It’ll be early next week if the kiln behaves.”
Emma looked at the shelves. The carved spoons had sold down to three; two of the wool throws were promised to customers who had paid deposits. “The invoice is due at the end of the month.”
“I know.”
She heard the defensive note in his voice and disliked it because it resembled her own. “I’m not asking you to send it before it’s ready. I need to know what I should tell people.”

Ben made his bowls and small trays in a converted outbuilding outside the city. Emma had met him there once, where shelves of unfinished work stood beside a kiln that appeared to have its own weather. He had told her, with some pride, that he did not scale up by outsourcing. She had admired the principle, then ordered as if the principle could be stretched without consequence.

“The glaze on the first batch crazed,” he said. “Not dangerously, but enough that I wasn’t happy sending it out. The replacement firing is on Monday. If I push it, I’ll send you something I wouldn’t want my name on.”
“I don’t want that either.” Emma rubbed the edge of the counter. “But I’ve got two customer deposits against the throws, and the spoons have been selling.”
“The throws aren’t mine, Emma.”
“No. I know.”

A brief silence followed. Ben had introduced her to the mill. She had put the line on her website with a photograph of its owner at the loom, after asking permission. The deposit had been taken for a product she expected to receive. The delay was not the customer’s fault, though the mill had not given Ben a firm date.
“I can send the bowls and trays first,” he said. “The spoons are ready. The wool is the problem.”
“Can you ship the finished pieces separately?”
“At my cost?”

The question was blunt, but not unreasonable. Emma had assumed that a small supplier could absorb the cost of her urgency. “I can pay the extra carriage for the finished work. I can’t promise the wool before I’ve had confirmation from the mill.”

“That’s fair.” His voice softened a little. “I’ve also got to change my terms. I can’t keep giving new stockists thirty days. Two shops have paid late, and I’ve been carrying the materials on my own card. From next month, first orders will be pro forma. After that, fourteen days.”
Emma’s stomach tightened. The current invoice was £1,460. The two delayed lines represented a larger order she had placed after the makers’ trail. “Does that apply to stock already ordered?”
“No. I’ll honour what we agreed. I’m telling you before you place another order.”

It was a courtesy, though it came dressed as a limit. Emma could have argued that thirty days had been part of the relationship. She could also see that supplier credit was still credit. Ben was not a department with a finance team and a reserve; he was one person paying for clay, fuel and firing time before a shop paid him.

“Could we split the outstanding invoice?” Emma asked. “I can pay half on the due date and half two weeks later. I’ll confirm dates in writing. If that doesn’t work, I’ll reduce the next order rather than leave you waiting.”
Ben was quiet. “I can do that once, if you send the first half on time.”
“I will.”
“And I’d rather you didn’t order deeper just because a Saturday went well.”
Emma let out a small breath. “That’s fair too.”
“Is it?”
“Not in the sense that I enjoy hearing it.” She heard the faintest laugh from him. “But yes.”

They agreed that Ben would send the ready spoons and bowls at his expense that afternoon, and Emma would pay the additional carriage. His next invoice would follow the new terms. The wool throws would remain on a separate purchase order, with no customer promised a date until the mill confirmed production.

After the call, Emma checked the cash-flow sheet she had made when she opened the shop. It was a simple forecast, with expected receipts and payments arranged by week. She had been updating it irregularly, which meant that the numbers were accurate in an historical sense and useless as a warning. She entered the expected Tuesday card settlement, the staged payment to Ben, the rent, wages, utilities, the refunds and the amount transferred to the VAT reserve.

The tax reserve was not a spare account. Her bookkeeper had explained that the business collected VAT on taxable sales and paid VAT on eligible purchases, then settled the net amount when due. Emma had kept a separate sum because she was new to the rhythm of it and did not want a future tax bill to masquerade as available cash. The reserve was healthy. The operating account was not.

Revenue for the first half of the month stood at £8,420, including VAT. The gross margin on those sales was approximately £3,500 before fixed and variable operating costs. Rent, business rates, wages, utilities and insurance consumed much of that; workshop materials, card fees, packaging and delivery added more. The shop was close to break-even on an accrual basis, but the cash timing made the week feel worse. Supplier invoices were payable before some of the stock had sold. The card processor settled in batches. A customer’s deposit was not profit, nor even fully free cash, while the promised item remained undelivered.

The next month’s rent was £1,650. Wages, including Emma’s modest draw, were due on Friday. She moved £420 into the tax reserve and left it there. The figure in the main account was £2,180 before the next card settlement and the first payment to Ben. Working capital was what remained to keep the shop trading between paying for things and being paid for them. It had become a narrow bridge.
Priya watched Emma print the updated cash-flow sheet. “Do you want me to reduce my shift next week?”
“No,” Emma said. “You’re needed.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”
Emma looked down at the forecast. “I don’t want you to subsidise a decision I made. I’ll review orders, not hours. If the figures say we can’t afford the rota, I’ll talk to you before I change it.”
Priya nodded, not reassured exactly, but acknowledged. “Then we need those figures every week.”
“Yes.”

Emma put a recurring appointment in the diary. She had once regarded admin as the dull interval between ideas. Now she understood that the interval was where obligations accumulated. Ben’s delay had not created the weakness in her plan. It had found it.

The finished spoons arrived on Monday, carefully packed. Emma sent Ben the agreed payment date in writing and paid the carriage that afternoon. She also emailed the customers who had placed deposits for the throws. She offered them the choice of a refund or waiting for a confirmed delivery date. One chose a refund. The other chose to wait, but asked Emma not to promise a week until the mill had done so.
Emma thanked her and amended the order notes. This time, the correction reached the person who needed it.

chapters.title: The Other Workshop
pages: Ruth’s announcement appeared on a Tuesday morning, shared by a customer who had attended one of Emma’s first workshops. The photograph showed a long worktable in the back room of Ruth’s homewares shop, with bundles of fabric arranged beside a bowl of scissors. The caption read: Visible mending for beginners. Two hours, materials included. Bookings now open.
