Emma read it twice, then once more as if the words might change into something less pointed. Ruth’s shop, The General Room, was six streets away and had been established for years. It sold furniture, lighting and gifts with the polished certainty of a place that had survived several versions of the neighbourhood. Ruth had once visited Emma’s shop before opening and complimented the display. Emma had taken the compliment as evidence of goodwill.
“She’s doing the same workshop,” Emma said.
Priya was matching supplier invoices to delivery notes. “She’s doing a mending workshop.”
“At the same price.”
“Two pounds less.”
“She’s copied the format.”
Priya looked up. “Have you seen who’s teaching?”

Emma opened Ruth’s post. The teacher was Lorna, an experienced textile artist whose work appeared in a regional craft directory. Emma had not approached Lorna. She had hired Sadie, who taught at a community centre and had been recommended by Mara. The two workshops were similar in title but not identical in content.
“It’s still direct competition,” Emma said.
“Yes.”

Priya’s agreement made Emma feel more unreasonable than a contradiction would have. She had spent the morning working on the booking page, carefully describing the session as an introduction to practical repairs rather than a demonstration of technique. Now Ruth’s post seemed to make the description look borrowed, though Emma had written it herself.
“She could have spoken to me.”
“About offering a class in her own shop?”
Emma shut the browser. “I know what you’re saying.”
“I’m not sure you do.” Priya placed an invoice in the paid pile. “You’re allowed to be cross. But we shouldn’t decide what her customers will do based on how cross you are.”

Emma went to the stockroom to check the wool throws, which had not arrived. It was an unconvincing task, but the shelves gave her something orderly to face. She had always assumed the shop’s advantage lay in curation: a coherent collection of objects, each with a maker and a story. Workshops extended that story into the room. If Ruth could offer the same experience, what exactly distinguished Emma’s version?

The question had the quality of an old workplace fear. She had spent years building plans that had to survive comparison with better-resourced teams. Her first response was to create more: more dates, more products, more communication. She could see the pattern and still feel the pull of it.
That afternoon, Ruth came in. She wore a dark green coat and carried a cardboard tube. After looking at the new shelves, she said, “Your window’s good.”
“Thank you.” Emma kept her hands on the till. “I saw your workshop post.”
“I wondered if you had.” Ruth unwrapped a poster proof and set it on the counter. “I’m putting a few up around the quarter.”
“You’re offering visible mending.”
“Yes.”
“So am I.”
Ruth did not pretend surprise. “I know. One of my customers said she’d been to your first session. It sounded well run.”
Emma searched for the right response and found three wrong ones. She chose the least generous. “It’s a small market.”

“It is. That doesn’t mean there’s room for only one class.” Ruth’s manner was courteous, but she had not come to apologise. “I spoke to six people who’d like to learn repairs. Four wanted evening sessions. One wanted a class that could accommodate a wheelchair. Your workshop is on a Saturday afternoon, isn’t it?”

Emma felt a small internal shift. The booking form had a question about access, but she had not thought to specify the height of the worktable or the route through the back room. Her room was narrow. She had described it as welcoming without asking whose body it welcomed.
“It is,” she said. “We’ve got one evening date under consideration.”
“I wasn’t aware of that.”
“It’s not confirmed.”
Ruth nodded. “I’m not claiming the territory. I’m responding to what people asked me for.”
“And the price?”
“Lorna’s fee is lower than yours, so I can charge less.”

Emma’s first impulse was to say that Sadie deserved a higher fee. She also knew she did not know Ruth’s costs, the arrangement with Lorna, or whether the lower price included the same materials. “We pay Sadie for preparation as well as teaching,” she said.
“That’s good practice.” Ruth touched the edge of the poster. “I pay Lorna for the full session and her planning time. I don’t want to race you to the bottom.”

There was no warmth in the exchange, but neither was there the hostility Emma had rehearsed. Ruth had listened to people, identified a different time and access need, and made an offer. That was not theft. It was market evidence.

After Ruth left, Emma searched her own enquiry log. Seven people had asked about evening sessions over the past two months. She had remembered the three from the event and dismissed the others as scattered interest. One customer had asked whether the workshop room was accessible and had received a vague reply. Emma had told herself she would follow up after the busy week.
“We need to answer that properly,” she said.
Priya was entering bookings into the new log. “Yes.”
“Not just ask if someone needs anything. We need to say what the room is actually like.”
“The entrance is level, but the toilet isn’t accessible. The table height is fixed. We can move the chairs.”
“And the turning space?”
“Not enough for every chair.”

Emma wrote the measurements down. It was uncomfortable to state limitations because she had wanted the room to be proof of her intentions. But a person planning to attend needed practical facts, not a reassuring adjective.

She called Sadie about an evening date and asked whether she would consider a smaller group with a lower fee per participant. Sadie said she could, provided the class remained a full two hours and the materials were not reduced. Emma asked the current customers whether evenings would suit them, without implying that a new session would be guaranteed. Three of the seven answered. Two could attend; one preferred a weekend.

The evidence was thin, but it was better than the conclusion Emma had drawn from Ruth’s poster. She would test one evening session, capped at six, before adding more. She would also speak with a local access group about whether a future class could be held in a more suitable venue.

She did not copy Ruth’s price. She calculated the teacher’s fee, materials, card charges and a share of the room’s fixed costs. At six places, the fee would need to be £36 to leave an adequate contribution. At four, the workshop would make little more than its direct costs. The booking page would say that the session would be confirmed once four places had been paid for, with a full refund if it did not proceed.
When Priya read the draft, she said, “That’s clearer.”
“It’s less enticing.”
“It’s clearer.”

Emma left the wording as it was. Competition had not taught her to be unique. It had made her look at what customers were actually asking for, and at the parts of her offer that she had mistaken for universal.

chapters.title: The Shape of a Week
pages: The week after the autumn trail, the shop did not empty, but it returned to its ordinary scale. Monday brought a customer looking for a birthday present, two people who wanted to collect repaired lamps, and a parcel of cards. Tuesday produced no sale before lunch. Wednesday’s takings were respectable. Emma had begun to understand that ordinary was not failure, though she still sometimes experienced it as a verdict.

She made a new rule for ordering. No product would be increased solely because it had sold well at an event. She would look at the previous eight weeks, the supplier’s lead time, minimum order quantity, payment terms and the stock already held. For a new line, she would place a small test order where possible. The rule did not forbid confidence. It required confidence to show its working.

The rule was tested that afternoon when a customer asked for more of Nisha’s blue-glazed cups. Emma had sold eleven at the trail. Only two had sold in the week afterwards. She had four left, with a further six on the way. Nisha’s minimum order was twelve, and a new batch would take a month.
“Can you let me know when you have more?” the customer asked. “I’m buying a present, but it doesn’t have to be today.”

Emma took her details, with permission, and promised to contact her if Nisha confirmed another batch. She did not collect a deposit. It seemed an almost absurdly small act of restraint, yet it felt like declining a possible sale.

That evening, Nisha replied about Mrs Finch’s dish. She had examined the photographs and agreed that the crack beneath the foot was not a normal variation. She offered to replace the piece and credited Emma for the wholesale cost. Emma told her she had already refunded the customer, then asked whether she could send the dish back so Nisha could inspect the firing fault.
“Yes, please,” Nisha wrote. “I’d rather see it than guess.”

Emma wrapped the dish, added the customer’s description, and sent it with the next returns parcel. She did not ask Nisha to refund the postage. It was part of treating the problem as shared without pretending that the customer should bear its cost.

The booking log was already changing the way the week felt. On Monday morning, Emma checked what had arrived over the weekend and assigned the enquiries. Priya answered the questions about class materials. Emma replied to a customer asking whether a textile workshop was suitable for someone with limited hand strength. She did not know the answer, so she asked Sadie, who proposed that the participant bring a preferred tool and said she could adapt the first exercise. Emma sent both details back. The customer booked one place.
“You got an answer within a day,” Priya said.
“We did.”
“You sound surprised.”
“I’m not surprised.” Emma closed the booking log. “I’m pleased.”
Priya gave her a look that suggested the distinction was not yet settled.

The evening mending workshop reached its minimum of four paid bookings three days before the deadline. Emma confirmed it and paid Sadie’s preparation fee. A fifth place sold the next morning. At £36 each, the gross revenue would be £180, including VAT. After the VAT element, the teacher’s fee of £92, materials at £8 per participant and card fees, the session would contribute only a small sum towards fixed costs. It would not transform the shop’s results. It would, however, test an evening time with a limited commitment and a clear cancellation point.

Emma had once been inclined to call a workshop successful if it sold out. Now she wanted to know whether people attended, whether the experience met what had been promised, whether the teacher was paid fairly, and whether customers would recommend it. The measure was less dramatic and more useful.

The week’s cash-flow review took place on Friday morning. Emma, Priya and her bookkeeper, Julia, sat around the back-room table, where the accounting laptop had to be balanced on a box of paper bags. Julia had sent a short monthly report and marked the difference between the till’s apparent abundance and the bank’s available balance.

“Revenue for the month to date is £10,160 including VAT,” Julia said. “The net sales figure, excluding VAT and refunds, is lower. Your gross margin is holding at about forty-one per cent, which is acceptable for this mix. But that’s before payroll, rent, rates, insurance, utilities and your other operating costs.”
“And the workshops?” Emma asked.

“They’re shown separately. They produce revenue, but the direct costs are also higher than on a lot of the stocked goods. Your first session made a modest contribution. The second was nearly break-even because you had to buy extra materials.”

Emma looked at the report. The number she had wanted from the trail now sat among other numbers, less luminous. She had made a gross profit from sales, but gross profit was not the same as profit after overheads. The month was not yet closed, and some invoices had not arrived. Their provisional operating result was close to zero before tax and Emma’s full compensation; the shop was trading, but it was not yet reliably paying for her labour in a way she considered sustainable.

“The bank balance is £3,060,” Julia continued. “That includes £650 received from the card processor yesterday. You have £1,100 in the tax reserve, which I would leave untouched. Rent is due on Monday. Ben’s first instalment is due next week, and wages are due before that.”
“So the business isn’t insolvent,” Emma said, too quickly.

Julia did not flinch. “No. But the working-capital margin is thin. You have commitments against cash that hasn’t arrived yet. The VAT reserve is prudent, not discretionary. And the customer deposits for the throws remain obligations until the goods are delivered or refunded.”
Priya looked at the printed booking calendar. “We can avoid adding another date until we know how this one goes.”
“Yes,” Emma said. She surprised herself by saying it without adding a defence.

They agreed that Emma would pause non-essential buying for three weeks, except for replenishment of proven bestsellers in small quantities. She would not reduce Priya’s shifts to disguise the cost of an over-order. They would review stock ageing, workshop attendance and enquiry conversion at the next weekly meeting. Emma would also contact the mill again, not to press for a date it could not guarantee, but to ask for an updated production estimate before she accepted further deposits.
After Julia left, Priya began stacking chairs. “You took the trail well,” she said.
“I took it too well.”
“You wanted it to mean the shop had arrived.”
Emma felt the accuracy of that. “I wanted one day to answer all the questions.”
“It answered some.”
“And made me ask the wrong ones.”
Priya set a chair against the wall. “That happens.”

Emma wanted to say that it could not happen again. Instead she picked up the workshop calendar and crossed out a date she had added without confirming the teacher. There was nothing heroic in the mark. The paper took it cleanly.

On Saturday, the shop opened at ten. A couple came in looking for a housewarming present and left with a bowl made by Nisha, after Emma described the crack issue and how it had been handled. The woman asked whether the maker would still be supplying the shop. Emma said yes, once the replacement batch had passed inspection.
“That’s straightforward of you,” the woman said.
“It ought to be.”

They bought the bowl. It was a small sale, and it did not prove that candour increased revenue. Emma entered it into the till, wrapped the object, and gave them the maker’s card. For once, she did not turn the moment into evidence for a larger claim.

The shop held its ordinary pace. Outside, the city moved towards the next event without asking what the previous one had taught her. Inside, Emma wrote the next supplier review into the diary, checked the bank forecast, and answered the last unanswered message in the log. The courage required was not the courage to begin again. It was the less flattering courage to continue at a size the evidence could support.

chapters.title: The Shape of the Week
pages: By Wednesday, Emma had begun to measure time in tasks she had not finished. The shop was open, the till balanced, the shelves faced towards the door; behind the counter, however, a box of unsorted delivery notes leaned against a crate of ceramic mugs, and three emails marked urgent had acquired the quiet menace of furniture.

Aisha was wrapping a customer’s purchase when the phone vibrated on the worktable. Emma glanced at it: Priya. The message was brief. The exhibition opened at seven. I know you said you’d try. It would mean a lot if you came.

Emma had said she would come. Priya had spent nearly a year organising a group exhibition in a room above a print studio, and the private view was not a casual drinks invitation. Emma knew this; she had listened to Priya discuss the work, the insurance, the hanging, and the difficulty of persuading artists to agree on a wall colour. She had even promised to bring flowers.

At five, a supplier rang to say a box of hand-thrown bowls had been misrouted. At half past five, the card terminal failed to reconcile with the till. Aisha found the missing transaction, but only after Emma had called the provider and listened to a recording that repeatedly thanked her for her patience. By the time the problem was settled, the flowers were still in a bucket beneath the counter.
“Go,” Aisha said, folding tissue around a small bottle of locally blended oil. “I can lock up.”
“I can’t leave you with the stock count.”
“I can do a stock count.”
Emma looked at her. Aisha’s expression was level, not hostile. That made it harder to dismiss.
“I said I’d help with the count,” Emma replied.
“You said you’d do it. You also said we’d talk about my hours before the end of the month.” Aisha tucked the bottle into a paper bag. “It is the end of the month.”

The customer left, carrying a gift Emma had not sold. For a moment, the shop was quiet except for the refrigerator’s small mechanical shudder. Emma had hired Aisha for a set number of hours, then asked her to stay late through the Saturday that had briefly suggested the business was becoming something more than a hopeful arrangement. She had paid the extra hours, but not yet addressed the fact that they were recurring.
“You’re right,” Emma said. The phrase came out as a defence before she could make it an apology. “Let’s sit down tomorrow.”
“Tomorrow I’m here until four.”
“Then four.”
Aisha put the wrapping paper away. “And tonight?”

Emma looked at the clock. The exhibition was across town. She could still go, though she would arrive after the speeches, perhaps after Priya had spent the evening watching other people arrive on time.
“I’ll close,” Emma said. “You’ve done enough today.”
Aisha nodded, neither grateful nor triumphant. Emma’s phone lit again, but she did not pick it up. The choice had been made; the cost was not improved by pretending it was inevitable.

She closed at six, carried the bucket of flowers to the back room and found the stems had begun to droop. The exhibition room was already dark by the time she reached it. Priya’s message arrived as Emma stood outside the locked print studio: I’m sorry you missed it. It went well. We’ll talk soon.
The word soon had no accusation in it. Emma found herself wishing it had. An accusation could be answered; disappointment had to be carried.

At home, her mother rang while Emma was eating toast above the sink. Her parents had not objected to the shop, exactly. They had asked questions about rent, pensions, and whether a person could really call herself self-employed if she spent half her day cleaning fingerprints from glass. Their concern was practical and, at times, so carefully phrased that it sounded like a verdict.
“You sound tired,” her mother said.
“It’s a busy week.”
“Every week seems busy.”
Emma stared at the dark window, where her own face floated over the street. “That’s because it is.”
“You don’t have to prove you can work harder than the job you left.”

The remark irritated her because it was true enough to be unusable. She said she was fine, and her mother did not insist. They spoke about a cousin’s new flat, then said goodbye with the tenderness of people who had decided not to press a sore place.

Sleep came in scraps. Emma woke at three thinking about the card settlement, then at five remembering the flower bucket. In the morning, she took out the cash-flow sheet she had been avoiding. The recent increase in takings had improved the week’s revenue, but it had not turned revenue into free money. Supplier invoices remained due; rent and utilities did not wait for a good Saturday. The small tax reserve was not working capital, and she had marked it separately for a reason.

At four, Aisha sat opposite her at the worktable. Emma brought the rota, the payroll records and a notebook. She did not begin with a speech about how much she valued Aisha. She began with the numbers.
“You’re contracted for sixteen hours,” she said. “You’ve averaged just over twenty for the last month. I’ve paid the extra hours, but I haven’t planned the business around them. That’s my mistake.”
“I like the work,” Aisha said. “I don’t like finding out on Tuesday that I’m doing Thursday as well.”
“I can offer eighteen regular hours from next month, at the same hourly rate, and I’ll review the rota six weeks after that. I can’t promise more pay today without pretending the cash is there.”
Aisha considered this. “Can we agree that extra hours are asked for, not assumed? And that I can turn them down?”
“Yes.” Emma wrote it down. “If the shop can sustain the higher hours, I’ll review the rate too. I won’t make a promise I can’t keep.”
“All right,” Aisha said. “I can work with that.”
It was not an embrace, nor a resolution to every strain. Emma felt relief, then shame at the relief. Aisha had required no confession of Emma’s private life, only terms clear enough to live inside.

That evening, Emma sent Priya a message that did not blame the shop. I’m sorry I missed it. I should have made the choice earlier. Can I take you for coffee next week and hear how it went? She pressed send before she could add an explanation that would make the apology about herself.

chapters.title: A Cleaner Story
pages: The proposal arrived through a contact Emma had met at a local makers’ market. Northline, a marketing agency with offices in London and Bristol, was assembling a Christmas campaign for a corporate client. They wanted a selection of independent products, a workshop and a polished account of the shop’s values. The fee, set out in a neat table, was large enough to alter the shape of the month.

Emma read the email twice, then forwarded it to herself, as if the second copy might reveal a condition the first had concealed. Northline would pay a fixed campaign fee on delivery, with a separate budget for products. The shop would provide the venue, coordinate makers, host the workshop and supply approved copy within three weeks. The client’s requested wording appeared below: “A fully sustainable collection, ethically sourced from zero-impact local producers.”

Emma opened the attached draft. One maker used reclaimed timber for some, but not all, of her work. The soap producer bought a portion of her ingredients from a UK wholesaler whose supply chain she could not fully verify. Aisha had made a careful note that the textile supplier used recycled fibres in one range, not across the whole catalogue. “Zero-impact” was not a description any of them had used.

The fee could cover the extra wage hours Emma had just agreed to, bring the working capital buffer back towards its intended level, and pay several overdue invoices without dipping into the tax reserve. It could also make the shop visible to customers who spent without scrutinising every price. She felt the attraction as a physical easing in her chest.

Northline’s account manager, Lewis, called that afternoon. He was courteous and unhurried. “The client wants a strong message,” he said. “They’re trying to move away from generic gifting. Your shop gives the campaign a human centre.”
“We can give them an accurate one,” Emma said.
“Of course. But ‘partly made with recycled fibres’ doesn’t travel as far as ‘sustainable’.”
“It may travel less far. It is also true.”
Lewis paused. “We’re not asking you to certify anyone. It’s campaign language.”
“If customers read it as a claim about the products, it is a claim about the products.”

He did not argue. Instead, he moved to the operational terms. The event would require two extra evenings of preparation, a Sunday workshop and a delivery of boxed sets to the client’s offices by a date that left little room for a supplier delay. Northline’s fee covered coordination, but not the additional staff hours or the cost of packaging. The client would approve the final invoice only after all items had been received and photographed.

Emma wrote the terms in the margin. The apparent fee was not the same as profit. Product costs, labour, transport and packaging would have to be deducted, and cash would leave the shop before the final payment arrived. Even if every task went well, the payment timing would put pressure on working capital.
“Could we change the wording and secure a deposit?” she asked.
“The client’s finance process doesn’t permit deposits,” Lewis said. “I can ask about the language, but I can’t promise they’ll accept a softer line. The timing is fixed.”
“And if a maker cannot meet the delivery date?”
“We’d need you to substitute something equivalent.”
Equivalent, Emma thought, was a word that could turn a maker into a unit and a promise into a box with a barcode.
She did not decide on the call. After closing, she set the draft beside the product files and asked Aisha to go through it with her. Aisha read the claims, then the delivery schedule.
“We don’t know that the client will pay late,” Emma said.
“No. We know they pay after approval.” Aisha turned the page. “That isn’t the same thing.”
“If we get the job, we could afford more regular hours.”
“If we get the job, we also have to do the job.”
The answer was sharp enough to make Emma defensive. She almost said that she understood. Instead, she asked, “What worries you most?”

“The Sunday. I’ve already been doing more than I expected. You’ve offered eighteen hours, which is good, but the schedule puts me here for late preparation and the workshop. The fee doesn’t say whether those hours are paid. And if we call everything sustainable, people may think we’ve checked things we haven’t checked.”
Emma looked at the page. She had been treating the proposal’s money as a solution and its obligations as details. “They’ve budgeted for the workshop assistant separately,” she said.
“Have they?”

Emma checked. The budget listed a facilitator’s fee, which would go to the maker leading the session. It did not list support staff. She had mentally counted the amount twice: once as payment to the facilitator, once as money available to cover Aisha. The mistake was small on paper and larger in the room.
“No,” Emma said. “They haven’t.”

She drafted a reply asking Northline to replace the broad claim with specific descriptions; pay a deposit sufficient to cover the products and direct costs; and agree to a separate, paid fee for the shop’s coordination and staff time. She offered a shorter schedule and named the products whose materials the makers could substantiate. The email took nearly an hour because each sentence seemed to invite a less honest version of itself.

Lewis called the next morning. “The client has decided to go with a supplier who can deliver the full campaign as briefed,” he said. “They need the language to remain simple, and they can’t change their payment terms this late.”
“I understand.”
“I did try.”
Emma believed him. That did not make the outcome better. “Thank you for asking,” she said.

After the call, she sat with the loss. The projected fee had not been profit; she knew that. Still, it had been a possible route through a narrow stretch, and now it was gone. There would be no sudden restoration of cash, no reassuring order large enough to quiet the question of whether the shop could sustain itself.
Aisha came in carrying the day’s post. “No?”
“No.”
“I’m sorry.”
Emma turned the proposal face down. “I was tempted to call their wording harmless. It wasn’t. And I missed that your hours were nowhere in the budget.”
Aisha set down the envelopes. “You noticed before we agreed.”
“Only because you asked.”
“That counts for something.”

It counted for less than the fee, more than Emma wanted to admit. She added the declined proposal to the folder of business decisions, not to celebrate the refusal but to remember its actual cost. In the evening, she updated the cash-flow sheet without inserting income that had never been earned.

chapters.title: The Winter Table
pages: The city’s Christmas market applications opened in September. Emma had intended to attend as a visitor, perhaps to speak with the organisers about the following year. Then a customer mentioned that a neighbouring street had hosted an independent winter market the previous December, and that the event had drawn a crowd despite the rain.

A week later, the organisers offered a larger slot in a converted hall: a weekend of local food, craft and demonstrations, with the shop responsible for a curated table and two workshops. The fee was substantial but not extravagant. The organisers’ photographs showed people shoulder to shoulder beneath strings of lights. Emma saw the Saturday figures from her own shop in that image: not as evidence of what had happened, but as evidence of what could happen again.

She was not alone in the decision. The market organiser was persuasive, and a potter whose work had sold well at the shop said she would make a special run of small pieces. A maker of woven decorations promised a discount if Emma ordered early. Even Aisha thought the event could be worth doing, provided the schedule was limited and the stock was chosen carefully.
Emma said yes before she had finished the cost sheet.

The decision seemed defensible when she completed it. The stall fee, transport, temporary display fittings and workshop materials were listed as fixed or event-specific costs. Product orders were recorded separately. She used the margin expected on each item, not its selling price, to estimate the contribution towards those costs. She included the card fee and a modest allowance for damaged or unsold stock. The calculation suggested that a reasonable level of sales would cover the event cost and leave a small contribution.

The flaw was in the words reasonable level. She had based it on the best Saturday the shop had seen, then raised that figure because the market would be busier than the shop. She did not obtain attendance data from the organisers. She did not ask how many visitors had bought from independent retailers the previous year. She had, in effect, used a burst of demand as a forecast.
Aisha noticed the stock order first. “You’re buying almost twice the quantity we sold in the first run,” she said.
“The event is twice the size.”
“The audience isn’t necessarily twice the size.”
“The organisers expect several thousand people.”
“Expect them to enter the hall, or expect them to buy from us?”
Emma heard the question as resistance. “If we go in looking understocked, we’ll waste the fee. We need a proper display.”
Aisha folded the order sheet. “A full display and an over-order aren’t the same thing.”

There it was: the old mistake in a newer coat. Emma was so intent on avoiding the appearance of uncertainty that she had started buying certainty in advance. She knew this, briefly. Then the potter sent a photograph of the special run, lined up on a board, and Emma felt committed not only by money but by the maker’s expectation.

She confirmed the orders. To keep cash available, she delayed payment to Ben, who had repaired a section of the shop’s front display and replaced a faulty latch. Ben’s invoice was due the following week. Emma told herself she would pay it as soon as the market takings cleared.
The phrase as soon as had become a form of borrowing.

She and Aisha spent two evenings planning the table. The products were arranged by use rather than by maker: gifts for the kitchen, objects for a desk, small things that did not require an occasion. Emma wanted customers to understand that the shop had made choices, not merely gathered stock. She wrote cards naming each maker and describing the materials as precisely as the makers had described them to her.
Aisha revised one card that read “locally made from sustainable wool” to “woven in Bristol using wool from a UK supplier”. The distinction was less elegant and more honest.
“You don’t have to make every sentence sound like a confession,” Emma said.
“I’m not. I’m making it say what we know.”
Emma left the card as Aisha had written it.

At home, Emma’s mother asked whether she could come to the event. Emma said of course, then heard the strain in her own voice and softened it. Her mother had offered to help before; Emma had refused, partly because she did not want unpaid family labour to make the business appear healthier than it was. She had not yet explained that the principle was about more than appearances.
“I’ll come and buy something,” her mother said. “That is not labour.”
“You don’t have to buy anything.”
“I know. I’m allowed to want a thing.”
Emma smiled, then asked her not to stay all day. The market was not a family outing, and she could not manage the worry of keeping everyone comfortable while she was trying to sell.

In the shop, she set aside the tax reserve and checked the operating account. The market’s advance payments would reduce working capital. The expected revenue, if it came, would restore some of it, but gross margin was not cash in hand until the card settlement arrived, and profit could not be declared before the costs were counted. She knew every distinction. Knowledge did not prevent her from wishing the figures would behave.
Ben rang about the invoice. “I can wait until Friday,” he said. “But I need to know where I stand. I’ve got materials to pay for.”
“I’m sorry. The market stock has taken more cash than I planned. I can transfer part on Friday and the balance next week.”
“Can you put that in an email?”
“Yes.”

He did not sound angry. He sounded like a tradesman who had learned to protect himself from clients’ optimism. Emma sent the email at once and paid a first instalment that afternoon. The cash balance looked smaller afterwards, though more honest.

The day before the event, a supplier rang to warn that one of the larger orders would arrive a day late. Emma asked whether the delivery could be split. It could, for a charge. She accepted the charge without calculating its effect on the event margin, because there was no time and because she had already decided that the display must be complete.

That evening, she and Aisha packed boxes until after closing. Aisha checked each item against the list. Emma kept moving between the list and the display, adjusting a stack of notebooks by centimetres. When Aisha asked whether they should stop, Emma said they were nearly there.

They were nearly there for another hour. When Emma finally went home, she realised she had not eaten since lunch. She slept badly, woke before the alarm and arrived at the hall with a certainty that had been assembled, piece by piece, from tasks completed rather than evidence gathered.

chapters.title: A Hall Full of People
pages: The hall was full by noon. The trouble was that it was full of people who had come to look.

They moved in clusters beneath the high windows, carrying coffee and paper bags from the food stalls. They paused at the shop’s display, admired the ceramics, read the maker cards and asked whether the woven decorations were available in other colours. A few made purchases. More said they would come back after they had seen the whole market, a promise delivered with the optimism of people who had no reason to suspect the day would defeat them.

Emma greeted everyone, explained the makers’ processes and kept the table tidy. She was good at the work when she was not trying to control its outcome. A customer asked whether the wool had been dyed locally. Emma did not know. She said so, then offered to ask the maker. The customer thanked her and bought a small dish instead.

Aisha ran the first workshop. It was well attended, though not full, and the participants made simple paper lanterns with local artist Rowan. Rowan received the agreed fee. Aisha had been paid for the hours on the rota, including the additional workshop time Emma had arranged in advance. It mattered to Emma that the event’s weakness should not be made Aisha’s unpaid problem.

By three, the display looked almost untouched. Emma began to rearrange it again. She moved the ceramics to the front, then moved them back when a child nearly knocked one over. Her mother arrived with a friend and bought a small woven coaster. She did not stay to help, and Emma felt grateful for that, though she wished she had been able to offer her a cup of tea.

At the neighbouring stall, a larger retailer had discounted gift sets and printed signs offering a market-only price. Their products were not local in the same way, but they were attractively boxed and inexpensive. A group of visitors compared the sets, then left with two.
“We can’t match that,” Aisha said quietly.
“I know.”
“I’m not saying we should.”

Emma checked the till. Revenue was below the mid-point in her estimate. The gross margin on each sale remained close to plan, but there were too few sales for that percentage to rescue the event. The fixed costs had not changed because footfall had been disappointing. The extra delivery charge had already reduced the contribution further.

At closing, the organisers thanked the stallholders for their participation. Emma did not ask whether the event would be repeated. She was carrying a box of unsold goods and did not trust herself to sound curious.

They packed the van slowly. Aisha wrote down the remaining stock and separated items that had been damaged from those that could return to the shop. Emma wanted to declare the event a failure before she had the final settlement. Aisha said, “We should count first.”
So they counted.

The final figures were not dramatic. That made them worse. The event had produced revenue of £1,460. The product cost of the goods sold was £690, leaving gross profit of £770 before the event-specific expenses. The stall fee, transport, display hire, workshop materials, additional delivery and card charges came to £1,090. The event had therefore made an operating loss of £320, before any allowance for Emma’s own time.

The unsold stock was not itself a loss: it remained saleable, though some of it would take months to move. It was, however, cash tied up in goods when cash was needed for wages, supplier invoices and the ordinary costs of opening the shop. The card settlement would arrive after the weekend. It would not arrive in time to pay everyone who had supplied the event.

Emma updated the cash-flow sheet at the kitchen table. She did not transfer money from the tax reserve. That money was not spare, and using it would turn a visible problem into a concealed one. She listed the next fixed costs, the variable costs already incurred and the supplier payments due. Then she wrote the current cash position at the top of the page and circled it, though a circle did not make it larger.

Ben’s remaining invoice was due. The potter’s balance was due on delivery. The woven-goods maker had agreed to split payment, but the first instalment was approaching. Aisha’s wages were protected by the payroll date; the business had to meet them. Emma calculated how much could be paid now and how much would need to be rescheduled. She had promised the potter a firm date. She did not want to revise it.

On Monday, she called the potter. “I ordered too much,” she said. “That’s my decision, not a problem with your work. I can pay the invoice in two instalments, starting Friday, and I will take the full order as agreed.”
There was a pause. “I’ve paid for the materials already,” the potter said.
“I know. I can pay half on Friday and the balance on the date we agreed for the final payment.”
“You said full payment on delivery.”
“I did.” Emma closed her eyes. “I’m asking to change that because I misjudged the cash. You can say no.”

The potter agreed, but only after Emma sent a written schedule and accepted that no further orders would be placed until the balance was paid. The condition felt fair. It also made visible the cost of treating a supplier’s trust as a flexible resource.

Ben was less willing to wait. He had already accepted a split payment. Emma transferred the balance from the operating account, leaving the cash position lower than she liked. His invoice was not the place to manufacture working capital.
When Aisha came in, Emma showed her the updated rota for the next fortnight. “I’m keeping your eighteen hours. I’m not going to cut them because I made a poor stock decision.”
“Can the shop afford that?”
“The next payroll is covered. After that, I need to bring sales and stock back into line. I’ll know more in two weeks. I won’t ask you to work extra hours without checking first.”
Aisha studied the sheet. “All right. But I need the rota to be dependable. I can’t keep planning around ‘perhaps’.”
“That’s fair.”
The sentence did not repair the strain. It gave it a shape.

That evening, Emma met Priya for coffee. She apologised again, this time without explaining the market, the stock or the supplier. Priya told her the exhibition had gone well and that two pieces had sold. Then she asked about the shop. Emma described the event, including the loss, without turning the story into a test of character.
“You always used to think a full room meant something was working,” Priya said.
“I still do, apparently.”
“A full room can mean people had somewhere warm to be.”
Emma laughed, though not because it was funny. She went home with no new money and no repaired certainty. She had, at least, stopped calling footfall demand.

chapters.title: The Count After
pages: For several days, Emma expected the market to keep failing after it was over. She imagined customers who had meant to return but had forgotten, makers who had heard she had over-ordered, and the hall’s empty table as a public judgement. None of these things happened. The shop opened on Monday, the doorbell sounded, and a customer asked whether the ceramic bowls came in a smaller size.

Emma answered the question without mentioning the event. She sold one bowl, then another. Their gross margin was as expected; the cash entered the settlement with the rest of the day’s card sales. It did not restore the event loss, but it belonged to the ordinary rhythm of the business rather than to her wish for a dramatic correction.

She began with the stock. Aisha and she sorted the market goods into four groups: items that had sold consistently in the shop, items that had sold only when demonstrated, items that needed new placement, and items that should not be reordered. They did not label the last group mistakes. Some of the products were good; the quantity had been wrong, or the occasion had been wrong, or both.

The largest order was put on a six-week review. The potter’s work was displayed in smaller groups, with the remaining pieces stored safely rather than crowded onto the shelves. Emma wrote to the makers whose products had been held for the event and gave them the revised sales information. She did not claim the market had been a success because the hall had been busy.
“People asked about colour,” Aisha said, reviewing the notes. “They didn’t buy the larger pieces. The small items sold better.”
“We could test a small colour range in the shop.”
“On sale or return?”
“Not without asking the maker.”

They asked. The maker agreed to a limited display of three pieces, with payment due on sale and a clear end date. Emma documented the arrangement. It was less efficient than ordering a large quantity at a discount, but the discount had not been free. It had required cash, storage and confidence in demand that she had not earned.

The next task was the cash forecast. Emma rebuilt it from actual transactions rather than from her previous assumptions. Revenue from the market was entered as earned. The cost of goods sold was separate from the cost of the unsold inventory. The event’s fixed expenses remained a loss; variable costs were recorded against the sales they had generated. The tax reserve remained untouched. The operating account, after the card settlement and scheduled payments, contained less working capital than she wanted but enough to meet the next payroll and rent.
She showed the revised sheet to Aisha. “There is no spare wage budget for additional hours this month,” she said. “Your eighteen contracted hours are in it. I can’t yet offer more.”
“I wasn’t asking for more this month,” Aisha said. “I was asking to know.”
“Then I should have told you before you had to ask.”
Aisha nodded. “Yes.”

They agreed to review hours at the end of the month, using actual sales and the next set of invoices. Emma added the review date to the rota, beside the hours. This did not make Aisha responsible for the shop’s cash position. It made the decision visible before it became a surprise.

Ben’s invoice was marked paid. Emma sent him a short note thanking him for accepting the split payment, without implying that his patience had been part of the service he had sold. He replied that he was glad the latch was working properly and that he would be available if the window needed attention before winter.

The small administrative exchanges unsettled Emma more than a dramatic confrontation might have. The business depended on people who did not owe her unlimited flexibility: an employee, makers, a repairer, a landlord, customers who could take their custom elsewhere. Good intentions did not settle invoices.

On Thursday, Priya visited the shop. She brought no flowers, which Emma was glad of; flowers would have seemed like a reward for making time at last. She looked around, bought a notebook and asked whether Emma had learned anything from the market.
“Not that busy rooms are meaningless,” Emma said. “Only that I can’t use them as evidence of sales.”
Priya turned the notebook over in her hands. “That sounds uncomfortable.”
“It is. It’s also cheaper than pretending.”

They arranged to have dinner the following week, on a day Emma would close at the usual time. Emma did not promise she would never miss another important thing. She wrote the date in her calendar and agreed not to book a workshop over it.

Her mother rang that evening. Emma told her about the loss before her mother could ask whether the event had gone well. There was a silence, then a question about whether the rent was covered. Emma answered with the figures: the next rent payment was included in the forecast; the market had reduced working capital; the tax reserve was still separate; no debt had been taken on. Her mother listened without converting the numbers into a moral.
“I’m glad you know where you stand,” she said.
Emma understood that this was not the same as approval. It was more useful.

She reviewed the event proposal one last time. The initial model had assumed a level of sales borrowed from the strongest Saturday at the shop. It had also treated the public’s presence as a proxy for willingness to buy. She changed the planning template. Future events would have a maximum stock commitment, a minimum break-even sales figure and an evidence check: previous attendance where available, audience fit, conversion assumptions and payment timing. If the organiser could not provide data, the uncertainty would be stated, not hidden beneath an optimistic average.

She also added a rule that seemed obvious once written: no event whose costs could not be met without touching the tax reserve or delaying an existing supplier invoice. There could be exceptions, but an exception would require a deliberate decision, not the momentum of a full-looking room.
Aisha read the new template the next morning. “This is better,” she said. “It still won’t tell us what people will do.”
“No.”
“But it might stop us ordering on the basis of what we hope they’ll do.”
“That’s the idea.”

They began planning a smaller winter evening in the shop: one maker demonstrating a process, a modest booking limit and no large stock order. The ticket price would cover the facilitator’s fee and materials. Any product sales would be additional revenue, not the assumption that made the event viable. Emma pencilled in a date, then checked it against Aisha’s contracted hours and her own calendar before confirming.

She had once believed commitment was proved by the size of the risk. Now she could see how easily risk became someone else’s unpaid labour, a maker’s delayed payment, or a friend waiting outside a locked door. That did not mean she would choose safety every time. It meant she would ask who paid for her courage when it went wrong.

At closing, she counted the till with Aisha. The cash total was ordinary. The card takings would settle in the usual time. They wrote down the figures, checked them against the sales record and locked the drawer. No revelation followed.

Outside, rain began to stipple the pavement. Emma turned off the window lights, then stopped with her hand on the switch. A small card beside the door named the makers whose work was inside. She straightened it by a fraction, not because the angle would alter the accounts but because it had slipped.
Then she locked the door and went home, carrying no heroic certainty with her. Only the week’s figures, a dinner date, and a decision to find out before she bought the next version of a good idea.

chapters.title: The Numbers on the Table
pages: Martin arrived before opening with a paper folder and no greeting elaborate enough to disguise its purpose. Emma had set out two cups of coffee, the ledger, and the spreadsheet she had been revising since the hall event. The spreadsheet was open on her laptop, a green cell announcing that the shop had made a profit in October. She had highlighted it.
“That,” Martin said, looking at the screen, “is not the number I want to discuss first.”

He put the folder beside her notebook. Outside, the city was in the particular grey of a morning that had not decided whether to rain. Aisha was in the stockroom, counting candles. Priya’s latest delivery—ceramics wrapped in reused paper—waited unopened by the counter.
“I know the last few weeks have been uneven,” Emma said. “But the events are starting to build—”

“I want to know whether you can keep the doors open through the uneven bit.” Martin pulled a chair towards him. “Not whether the idea is good. Not whether the October event felt encouraging. How much cash is available, what must leave the account, and when?”

Emma turned the laptop towards him. She had been proud of the spreadsheet until he asked for the bank balance rather than the projected margin. She found it: £8,460 in the business account that morning.
“That includes the money due for the next rent payment?” he asked.
“It includes everything in the account.”
“That isn’t the same answer.”

She knew. The next quarterly VAT payment was not yet due, and she had been treating the whole balance as reassurance. She wrote the figures in her notebook: £2,140 estimated VAT reserve; £1,300 set aside for income tax and corporation tax obligations, subject to the accountant’s final calculation; £1,850 for the next rent and service charge, due in three weeks. The sums were not separate bank accounts, but they were promises the money had already made.
“So available cash after those commitments is £3,170,” Martin said. “And you have invoices due?”
“£2,460, mostly suppliers. The payment dates are staggered over the month.”
The number she had wanted to present as proof of survival changed shape. There was cash, and there was cash that could safely be spent. They were not synonyms.
Martin drew a line down the page. On one side he wrote PAST; on the other, NEXT.

“The original fit-out, the first sign, the shelving that turned out to be too shallow—those are sunk costs. They matter to the story of how you got here, but they cannot be recovered by keeping a bad decision alive. The question is not how much you have spent. It is what the next month costs, and what each option returns.”

Emma looked at the October result again. Revenue had been £11,820, including the hall takings and workshop bookings. Cost of goods sold had been £5,790, giving a gross margin of £6,030, just over fifty-one per cent. After rent, service charge, utilities, insurance, card fees, wages, marketing, and other operating costs, the spreadsheet showed a small operating profit before tax.
“It doesn’t include my proper wage,” she said.
Martin nodded. “Nor does a profit on paper refill the till on the day the rent leaves.”

She had counted her own unpaid hours as evidence of commitment. In the accounts, they were invisible; in her life, they had become an accumulating liability. The October figure was real, but it was not a verdict.

They sorted costs into columns. Rent and service charge came to £1,850 monthly. Insurance, software, basic utilities, and accountancy averaged £510. Aisha’s contracted hours, including employer costs, averaged £1,420. Marketing and other regular spending were about £240. Fixed costs were therefore roughly £4,020 a month, before Emma paid herself and before stock, card fees, or event materials.

“Your gross margin varies,” Martin said. “The shop range is not all fifty-one per cent. Some products give you more; some, especially the work you chose to stock because it was beautiful, give you less.”

Emma opened the product report. The best-selling locally made soap had a healthy margin. The large stoneware pieces tied up money and sold slowly. Gift bundles moved, but required extra packaging time. She had ordered the ceramics in breadth because a full shelf looked like confidence.

“At an average gross margin of fifty per cent, you need about £8,040 in monthly sales to cover those fixed costs,” Martin said. “That is break-even before your wage, tax, debt repayments, or a cash buffer. If your margin slips to forty-six per cent, the sales required rise to about £8,740.”
“And if workshops contribute?”
“Then calculate their contribution after the tutor, materials, payment fees, and the time you spend preparing. Don’t count the whole ticket price as profit.”

Emma shut the product report. She had been assuming that the hall’s attendance meant a steady stream of new customers, that longer opening hours would catch them, and that people who admired a product would eventually buy it. Each assumption had been dressed as a forecast.
“I thought weekday footfall would climb after Christmas,” she said. “I thought the range needed to look abundant. I thought I could keep putting my own pay off until the shop settled.”
Martin did not soften his face to reward the admission. “Those are three different risks. Which one can you test?”

They made a thirteen-week cash forecast, beginning with available cash of £3,170 after commitments and unpaid supplier invoices. They put in rent, wages, remaining supplier payments, utilities, tax dates, expected card settlements, and cautious sales assumptions. They did not include a hypothetical January rush. With current opening hours and purchasing habits, the cash line dipped below zero before the end of the forecast.
“It’s a forecast, not a prophecy,” Martin said. “But it is telling you something.”
Emma looked at the red line. The spreadsheet’s earlier green cell remained visible behind it, still true, still insufficient.
“I’ve been using revenue to comfort myself,” she said.
“Then stop asking revenue to do a job it can’t do.”
Aisha emerged from the stockroom carrying a clipboard. Emma felt the first impulse to close the laptop, to protect her from a picture that might alarm her. Instead, she moved the chair out.
“We need to talk about what this means for the work,” Emma said. “Not today as a decision. Today as the facts.”
Aisha set down the clipboard. “Good,” she said. “Because I’ve been doing sums too.”

chapters.title: What We Owe Each Other
pages: Priya came in at eleven with a box of small bowls and a face that suggested she had already heard something. She had not; the face was her ordinary expression when an invoice had been paid late.
Emma asked her to stay. Aisha closed the stockroom door, though not all the way. Martin remained by the table, his folder shut.

“I want to explain the position before anyone has to infer it from a delayed payment,” Emma said. “The bank balance is £8,460, but after tax reserves and the next rent, and with £2,460 in supplier invoices due, only £3,170 is uncommitted. The forecast under the current model goes negative within thirteen weeks.”
Priya put one hand on the box. “You have my invoice in that figure.”
“Yes. I should have called you before today.”
“You should.”

The directness stung because it was not unfair. Emma had waited, hoping that the next batch of sales would turn uncertainty into an acceptable conversation. Instead, silence had left Priya to wonder whether the shop’s delay was a judgement on her work.

Aisha took out her own notebook. She had tracked quiet periods, customer questions, and the hours spent preparing workshops. Emma had asked her to keep notes, but had not asked to see them for three weeks.

“We’re spending time displaying stock that doesn’t sell,” Aisha said. “The big bowls get handled, admired, and put back. We’ve sold two in six weeks. People ask for smaller pieces under thirty pounds, and we keep running out of the soap and the printed cards.”
“The bowls are part of the shop’s identity,” Emma said, then heard how quickly she had chosen identity over evidence.
“They’re also almost four hundred pounds of cash sitting on the shelf,” Aisha replied. “I’m not saying they’re bad. I’m saying we can’t afford to treat admiration as demand.”

Priya glanced at the box. “If you reduce ceramics, I need to know whether you’re reducing my work or changing the terms. I planned materials for the next order. I can take back three pieces on consignment, but I can’t keep making stock on the assumption you’ll take it later.”

Emma felt the old defensive explanation assemble itself: she had promised local makers a platform; she had built the shop around a careful selection; the range was meant to be an invitation. She let the explanation pass without giving it the floor.
“I ordered too broadly,” she said. “I was wrong to call that commitment. I’m sorry I let the invoice sit while I tried to make the numbers more pleasant.”
Priya’s expression did not alter much. “An apology doesn’t tell me when I’m paid.”
“I can pay £700 on Friday and the balance by the twenty-fifth. If the cash forecast changes, I’ll tell you before either date. I won’t ask you to finance the shop.”

Priya considered this. “I can accept that schedule, but not a further delay without a conversation. For future orders, I’d rather agree a smaller quantity and a review date. I can’t offer consignment across the range.”
“That’s reasonable.”
“It isn’t generosity,” Priya said. “It’s a business arrangement that might work for both of us.”
Emma wrote down the dates. She had once heard firmness as rejection. Now she could hear the shape of a boundary: inconvenient, clarifying, and more respectful than an open-ended promise.

Aisha turned her notebook so they could see the records. On the two workshop evenings, ticket revenue had been £1,120. After paying tutors, materials, and fees, the contribution had been £438, before the cost of Emma’s planning time. The hall event had brought revenue and attention, but a portion of its takings had gone to the venue and stall costs. It had not, as Emma had loosely described it, “paid for the month.”

“The workshops work better when we sell them as specific skills,” Aisha said. “People booked the visible-mending session because they knew what they would leave with. The general making evening got fewer bookings.”
“The general evening was meant to build community,” Emma said.

“It might have. But we don’t have evidence it does, and we still have to pay the tutor.” Aisha paused. “Also, I can’t keep taking extra hours at short notice and then find out later whether they were within the budget. I need the rota agreed, and I need my hours paid on time.”
There was no accusation in the last sentence, only a record. Emma had asked Aisha to behave like a partner when work expanded, while keeping her outside the decisions that produced it.
“You’re right about the rota,” Emma said. “I’ll set the hours we can afford and ask before I change them. No unpaid event preparation.”
“And I want to see the numbers each month. Not every private detail, but the sales, stock, and workshop results.”
Martin had been silent. Now he said, “If you give people responsibility for the outcome, they need enough information to do the work responsibly.”

Emma nearly answered that she was the owner and carried the risk. It was true. It was also the sentence she had used to keep every decision close to herself, including decisions she had no time to perform well.
“You can see the monthly trading report,” she told Aisha. “And you can challenge the assumptions.”
“I already do,” Aisha said. “You don’t always hear them.”

The words landed with more force than a raised voice. Emma looked at the empty cup between them. She had imagined that accountability would feel like admitting failure. In practice it felt more like being asked to stop making other people pay for her pride.

They agreed on the immediate actions: pay Priya on the dates promised; pause broad ceramic orders; keep only measured quantities of slower lines; protect Aisha’s contracted hours; and review workshop contribution after each session. No one said that these measures would save the shop.
When Priya lifted the box again, Emma offered to carry it to the shelf. Priya did not hand it over.
“I’ve got it,” she said, not unkindly. “Just tell me before the next order what you actually need.”
“I will.”
It was a small promise, and for once Emma wrote it beside a date.

chapters.title: A Smaller Measure
pages: The next Tuesday, Emma took half the display down. She did not call it a refresh. She moved the large ceramics into a single cabinet, put the smaller pieces where customers could reach them, and left a patch of bare wall that made the shop look less like the picture she had first imagined.
Aisha watched her carry a tray of bowls to the stockroom. “Are you keeping those for a later display?”
“No. I’m listing them for sale at the price we need, not the price I wish they justified.”

They agreed a modest reduction on three pieces and an online photograph of the rest. The aim was not to turn them into a bargain-bin story, but to recover cash without pretending the original order had been wise. Emma put the cost price, current selling price, and expected margin on a sheet for each item. She found that two pieces would still make a reasonable gross margin at a small discount; one would barely cover its cost and card fees.
“That one can wait for a customer who wants it,” Aisha said. “It doesn’t have to be the centre of the shop while it waits.”

Emma called Priya that afternoon. She proposed a three-month trial: smaller orders of the designs customers had actually bought, with an agreed minimum, payment dates, and a review after six weeks. Priya would take back two unsold pieces at cost, but not the larger bowl Emma had hoped to return.
“I can’t absorb every risk in your range,” Priya said. “The glaze and the firing cost me the same whether you sell it or not.”
“I understand. I’m not asking you to.”

They revised the quantities and signed the updated order by email. The agreement was less comfortable than consignment, but more honest. Emma paid the first £700 on Friday as promised and sent Priya the remittance note before she asked.

The change in opening hours was harder. Monday and Tuesday had been open until six, though the till records showed long stretches with no sale. Emma wanted to keep the hours because a closed door seemed to announce retreat. Aisha showed her the last eight weeks’ sales by hour, separating revenue from the contribution left after product cost.

“If we close two hours earlier on Tuesday and use that time to prepare the paid workshops, the lost sales are likely to be lower than the extra staffing and operating costs,” Aisha said. “We should try it for four weeks, not declare it forever.”

Emma agreed. She put the revised hours on the door and online. A customer complained that Tuesday evenings were the only time she could browse after work. Emma offered to hold items for her and invited her to the monthly Saturday late opening. The customer accepted the reservation but not the invitation. Both responses were useful.

The workshops became shorter, priced more clearly, and limited to eight places. Emma had previously treated a full room as the measure of success. Now each booking page stated what the participant would learn, what materials were included, and what would happen if a session did not reach its minimum number.

For the first visible-mending workshop, six people paid £42 each. The tutor received £180; materials cost £58; payment fees were £7.50. The contribution before Emma’s administration time was £6.50 per ticket, or £39 in total. It was not a fortune, but it was no longer represented as one. Emma and the tutor reviewed the fee together before scheduling another.
“I can make the next one work if we use the offcuts and set the tutor fee for the full session,” the tutor said. “But not if I’m expected to bring supplies on speculation.”

Emma agreed the fee in writing and paid it within two days. She also changed the minimum from four bookings to six, cancelling early rather than risking a last-minute loss. The first time she cancelled, one customer was disappointed. Emma refunded her promptly and offered an alternative date; the customer booked the next one.

In the shop, they gave more space to products priced below thirty pounds: soap, small paper goods, mending kits, and locally printed cards. They did not pretend these had been a strategic revelation. Customers had been asking; the staff had been hearing; Emma had been slow to treat the pattern as data.

The partnership with the neighbourhood library began less neatly. Its organiser wanted a free evening event using the shop after closing, with a small makers’ demonstration and refreshments. Emma said yes before asking who would pay for staff time, materials, and cleaning.
Aisha caught the omission while they were drafting the plan. “If it’s free to attend, somebody is still paying to make it happen.”

Emma called the organiser back. They agreed that the library would cover the demonstration fee and refreshments, while the shop would provide the room for two hours and be named on the booking page. Emma budgeted staff time and set a clear cap on materials. The library could not pay a room hire charge, but it could provide volunteers for the door and share the event with its mailing list.

The arrangement was not a sales guarantee. It was a controlled experiment in reaching people who might not enter a shop alone. Emma made a simple tracking code for purchases linked to the event, with no discount that would make the figures hard to interpret.

They also tested a Saturday pop-up at a community market. The stall fee was £68; transport and extra packaging came to £31. Revenue was £412, with a gross margin of £218. After direct costs, the day made £119 before wages and preparation time. It was a useful result, not proof that markets could replace the shop.

At the end of four weeks, Emma printed the results rather than saving them for an imagined time when they would look more decisive. Sales had been lower on the shortened Tuesday, but the lost contribution was £74. Reduced staffing and utility costs attributable to those hours were about £112. The change had improved the monthly position by roughly £38, before any effect on workshop preparation.

The figure was small enough to be unglamorous and large enough to matter. The more important result was that the new hours could be communicated honestly and reviewed rather than defended as a statement of belief.
Aisha read the sheet, then pointed to the Saturday figures. “You’ve included the stall revenue under shop sales.”
Emma frowned. “It came through the same account.”
“The account is where the cash went. It doesn’t tell you where the sale happened.”

They changed the report. Emma thanked her without making the correction into a test of loyalty. The report now separated shop, workshop, online, and pop-up revenue, with direct costs shown beneath each.

When they locked up, there was less on the shelves, less certainty in Emma’s voice, and more usable information between them. She was not yet sure whether the shop could support her. She was beginning to see that the question had to be answered by a model that did not depend on pretending every experiment was a success.

chapters.title: An Offer with Edges
pages: The email arrived from North Quay House on a Thursday morning. Its director had attended the hall event and later bought a set of locally printed notebooks for a client reception. He wanted Emma to supply welcome gifts for a programme of corporate gatherings: eighty packages across four dates, each containing products from at least three local makers.

The proposed contract was worth £12,800, excluding VAT. North Quay would pay thirty days after delivery. It wanted consistent packaging, a single point of contact, and a twenty per cent reduction on the retail prices. In return, it offered a twelve-month preferred-supplier agreement and permission to use the House’s name in the shop’s marketing.
Emma read the message twice. The sum looked substantial beside the shop’s weekly takings. Then she read the payment terms again.
She asked Martin to come in, and invited Aisha to the meeting. Priya could not attend but agreed to review the product proposal by phone.

Their cost estimate was sobering. The products would cost about £6,160 at maker prices. Packaging and assembly materials would add £720. Delivery across the city and administration were estimated at £460. The total direct cost would be £7,340, leaving £5,460 before staff time, overhead, and tax. The apparent gross margin was about forty-three per cent of revenue, lower than the shop’s recent average.
“That doesn’t mean it’s a bad contract,” Martin said. “It means you price the work you’re actually doing. Who funds the stock before they pay you?”

The makers wanted deposits. Priya could supply the ceramics for one delivery at a time, but required payment before firing the next batch. The printmaker asked for fifty per cent up front. North Quay’s thirty-day terms meant Emma could be financing several thousand pounds of goods before the first invoice cleared.
Emma updated the cash forecast. If the contract ran as proposed, working capital would be short by around £3,800 at the point of highest exposure, even before unexpected breakages or delayed payment.
“The revenue is not the same thing as cash available,” Aisha said. “And the work lands in the same weeks as the shop.”
Emma had imagined the contract as a door opening. Aisha was looking at the hours required to carry the boxes through it.

They called North Quay’s director together. Emma asked whether they could split delivery into four invoices, with a thirty per cent deposit on each date and the balance payable within fourteen days. She also asked for a smaller first run, priced at the agreed margin, before committing to the year.

The director was courteous and firm. “Our procurement system is built around thirty days. We can pay a deposit for the first batch, but the preferred-supplier agreement would need exclusivity within the borough, and we would need approval over the final product mix. It is a sizeable account, Emma. We need consistency.”
“Would exclusivity apply to independent shops as well as other corporate clients?”
“To any retail or hospitality channel in the borough for the products in the package. We would not want the same items available elsewhere.”
Emma wrote that down. It was not an offensive demand. It was a commercial one, and it would give North Quay authority over where local makers could sell work they had made.

Aisha asked what would happen if a product sold out or a maker could not meet a delivery date. The director said substitutions would require approval. Emma imagined explaining to Priya that the next batch of her bowls belonged, in practice, to a purchasing department.
After the call, Emma spoke to Priya. Priya was willing to make a small batch at a fixed wholesale price, provided payment arrived before production. She was not willing to grant exclusivity.
“They’re asking you to promise control you don’t have,” Priya said. “You can promise what you buy. You can’t promise where I won’t sell the rest of my work.”
“I don’t want to bind you to that.”
“Then don’t.”

Emma and Aisha reviewed a revised proposal. They offered a pilot of twenty packages for one date, with a thirty per cent deposit, final approval limited to the particular items ordered, and payment within fourteen days of delivery. The price would be £3,200 excluding VAT. The direct costs were estimated at £1,835, leaving £1,365 before labour and overhead. They included an assembly fee rather than treating Emma’s time as free.

North Quay declined the shorter payment term and the removal of borough-wide exclusivity. It countered with a one-year agreement, a small first-order deposit, and the same control over product selection.

“The account would be valuable,” Martin said after the call. “But value is not permission to ignore the conditions. If you accept, you should know what you are trading and how much of the risk you can bear.”

Emma sat with the contract draft while the shop moved around her. A child asked Aisha whether the notebooks came in blue. The card machine beeped. Someone upstairs in the neighbouring office dragged a chair across the floor. The scale of the offer did not make the ordinary work disappear; it threatened to take more of it away from the shop.

She worked through three versions of the forecast. With the contract, the first month could show a strong revenue figure and still require cash she did not have. A delay in one corporate payment would leave her exposed to makers, while the exclusivity clause could narrow the shop’s range and undermine the relationships that gave it a reason to exist. The contract could stabilise the account, but it could also turn the business into a fulfilment service governed by a client whose priorities were not hers.
“I’m tempted because I’m frightened,” she said to Martin. “That doesn’t make the offer wrong. It makes my judgement suspect.”
“Fear is information,” he replied. “It is not a decision.”

Emma declined the preferred-supplier agreement. She thanked the director, explained that the exclusivity and payment terms were not workable, and left the door open to a single, properly funded pilot if the conditions changed. She sent the email before she could spend another week treating indecision as diligence.

The relief that followed was not clean. The shop still had a cash problem. She had turned down a large number, and some part of her continued to calculate what might have happened if she had accepted.
Aisha read the sent message. “You didn’t say we’re too small,” she said.
“We are small.”
“Yes. But that wasn’t the reason.”
Emma closed the contract file. For the first time, the refusal felt less like a defence of an image and more like a limit she could explain.

chapters.title: A Room That Could Continue
pages: The rent review came in the form of a letter from the property agent. The landlord was prepared to discuss a break clause and a smaller footprint, but not to reduce the rent for the existing unit. The room at the back—the one Emma had used for storage, packing, and workshops—could be separated with a new internal door and leased to another tenant. The monthly saving would be £620 after a modest contribution to the partition costs.

The offer required a decision within six weeks. Emma looked at the room’s folding tables, boxes of packaging, and the wall where the first workshop participants had pinned their work. Giving it up felt like losing a piece of the shop’s original promise. Keeping it, however, meant paying for space that was often empty.

Martin asked her to measure actual use. Aisha had already kept a calendar: eleven workshop sessions in three months, four evenings of private events, and regular packing work. Several sessions had used the library or the market instead. The room mattered, but not every day, and its importance did not prove that the current arrangement was affordable.

They built a revised monthly model. The smaller retail unit would still carry rent, service charge, utilities, insurance, software, and accountancy. Aisha’s hours would be reduced by agreement to a reliable part-time rota, not varied from week to week according to Emma’s anxiety. Emma would work two paid days a week as a freelance product and communications consultant, retaining one existing client from her corporate career and seeking no more work than she could deliver without neglecting the shop.

Her consulting income would be separate revenue, not shop sales. It would not improve the shop’s gross margin, and it would not be used to disguise a loss in retail. It could, however, pay part of Emma’s personal living costs, reducing the immediate pressure to draw an unsustainable wage from the shop.

The model assumed monthly shop revenue of £7,500, workshop revenue of £1,000, and a modest £400 from pop-ups, with no corporate contract. At an estimated weighted gross margin of forty-nine per cent, those activities would contribute about £4,361 after product and direct event costs. The reduced fixed costs were forecast at £3,250, leaving roughly £1,111 before Emma’s shop pay, tax, and any exceptional expenses.
“That isn’t a comfortable surplus,” Martin said.
“No,” Emma said. “But it’s not counting my consulting as shop profit, and it doesn’t depend on selling eight thousand pounds’ worth of stock every month before we buy the next order.”

The forecast still contained risk. A soft month could erase the projected contribution. The shop would need to maintain working capital for stock, tax, and rent; the VAT reserve would remain untouched; and supplier payments would follow written terms rather than hoped-for sales. Emma set a minimum cash threshold of £5,000, including tax reserves but excluding money already committed to invoices. If the business fell below it, they would stop discretionary purchasing and reassess the model before the next quarter.

They agreed measures to track weekly: sales by channel; gross margin by product group; stock older than ninety days; workshop contribution after tutor fees and materials; cash available after reserves and liabilities; and hours actually worked by Emma. She added one measure not found in the accounts: whether she had worked two consecutive days without a closing-time conversation about a crisis she could have prevented.
“That one is subjective,” Aisha said.
“It’s a measure of me, not the business.”
“Then keep it. But don’t use it instead of the numbers.”
Emma smiled. “I won’t.”

Priya agreed to continue under the smaller-order arrangement. She would supply a tested range of small bowls and cups in batches of six, with dates and prices confirmed before production. She declined to take on additional workshop demonstrations without a fee that covered preparation as well as the session itself. Emma accepted. They scheduled one paid demonstration for the following month and left the possibility of more open.

The landlord accepted the separation of the rear room, subject to the partition and a new tenant. Nothing was signed until the agent confirmed the details. Emma did not treat the saving as certain cash before it was real. She and Aisha cleared the storage shelves anyway, labelling what would remain in the shop, what could be sold, and what was rubbish.

One afternoon, a customer asked whether the shop would still run events. Emma could have said yes in the bright, absolute way she once used to quiet a difficult question. Instead she explained that the large room would go, but the shop would keep smaller workshops, partner events, and occasional off-site sessions.
“That might suit me better,” the customer said. “I never liked being in a room with twenty people.”
It was not a survey result, and Emma did not turn it into one. She wrote down the comment with the date.

The change would take time. For the first month they would still pay the old rent while the new tenant’s lease was completed. The partition cost was £900, paid from the business account only after protecting the tax reserve and scheduled supplier payments. They planned the move around normal trading, not a dramatic relaunch. The shop would stay open, with a sign explaining the revised workshop programme and a list of dates customers could book.

On the last evening before the room was cleared, Aisha found the first event plan pinned behind a shelf. It was covered in hopeful estimates and handwritten revisions. Emma had written “full house?” beside the expected attendance. Aisha read it and looked at her.
“You really thought a full room would solve everything.”
“I thought it would prove I hadn’t misread the people who came.”
“They came,” Aisha said. “That part was true.”
Emma folded the page. “And it didn’t mean what I needed it to mean.”

They carried the folding tables through the shop and loaded them into the borrowed van. The walls looked bare, but not abandoned. There would be a smaller room for retail, fewer products selected with greater care, paid workshops with clear costs, a part-time employee whose limits were respected, and consulting work that was not passed off as evidence of the shop’s success.

The business might still fail. The forecast could be wrong in either direction. Emma knew now that persistence could be a form of courage, but it could also be a way of refusing new evidence. She did not have to call every limit a defeat, or every risk an act of faith.

At the front door she checked the lock, then checked the cash report in her notebook. The balance was not generous. It was sufficient for the next set of obligations, provided they followed the plan and revised it when the facts changed.

In the morning, they would open the smaller shop. Emma would work there for the first half of the day, then leave for a consulting meeting she had scheduled without apology. The arrangement was neither the business she had once pictured nor a promise that it would prosper. It was work that had room for other people, room for correction, and—at last—room for her to go home.
